title: 1.7 Proof by induction
text:
重要Syllabus objective



Use the method of mathematical induction to establish a given result.
题目可以涉及有限和、递推数列、不等式、导数或矩阵幂；证明结构相同，但 inductive step 的运算对象不同。




设命题为 \(P(n)\)，起始整数为 \(n=n_0\)。完整证明必须包含：

Base case: 验证 \(P(n_0)\)；
Inductive hypothesis: 假设 \(P(k)\) 对某个 \(k\ge n_0\) 成立；
Target: 明确 \(P(k+1)\) 应是什么；
Inductive step: 只使用 \(P(k)\) 与已知事实推出 \(P(k+1)\)；
Conclusion: 写出由 mathematical induction，\(P(n)\) 对所有 \(n\ge n_0\) 成立。

\[
P(n_0),\; P(k)\Longrightarrow P(k+1)
\;\Longrightarrow\;
P(n)\text{ for every integer }n\ge n_0.
\]









提示Proof template



Base case. When \(n=n_0\), show that LHS = RHS (or that the stated inequality is true).
Hypothesis. Assume the result is true for \(n=k\), where \(k\ge n_0\):
\[
P(k).
\]
Step. For \(n=k+1\), begin from the side that contains the \(k\)-case, apply the hypothesis, and simplify until the target \(P(k+1)\) is obtained.
Conclusion. Therefore \(P(k)\Rightarrow P(k+1)\). Since \(P(n_0)\) is true, the result follows by mathematical induction for all integers \(n\ge n_0\).





If
\[
S_n=\sum_{r=1}^{n}f(r)=F(n),
\]
then the \((k+1)\) case begins with
\[
S_{k+1}=S_k+f(k+1).
\]
Use the hypothesis \(S_k=F(k)\), then show
\[
F(k)+f(k+1)=F(k+1).
\]
Do not assume the target \(F(k+1)\) at the beginning of the inductive step.



For \(u_{n+1}=g(u_n)\) and a proposed formula \(u_n=F(n)\), assume \(u_k=F(k)\) and write
\[
u_{k+1}=g(u_k)=g(F(k)).
\]
The target is \(F(k+1)\). The recurrence, not the proposed answer, must be the starting point.



For an inequality, the hypothesis supplies a bound rather than an equality. Every multiplication or division must respect signs. A typical step is
\[
A_{k+1}=c_kA_k>c_kB_k\ge B_{k+1},
\]
where the proof must explain why \(c_k>0\) and why the second comparison holds.
The base case must use the first value for which the statement is claimed, which need not be \(1\).



If a formula is proposed for \(D^n[f(x)]\), then
\[
D^{k+1}[f(x)]=\frac{d}{dx}\left(D^k[f(x)]\right).
\]
Differentiate the expression supplied by the hypothesis and simplify to the target with \(k\) replaced by \(k+1\).



For a proposed expression \(A^n=M_n\), use
\[
A^{k+1}=A^kA=M_kA.
\]
Carry out the matrix multiplication explicitly and transform every entry into the corresponding entry of \(M_{k+1}\). Do not treat matrix multiplication as elementwise multiplication.




Checking several numerical cases gives evidence, not proof.
Proving only \(P(k)\Rightarrow P(k+1)\) is insufficient without a valid base case.
A correct base case alone does not establish later cases.
The conclusion must state the domain, such as all positive integers or all integers \(n\ge4\).

title: 1.7 Proof by induction
text:
2. Textbook Examples
本节保留教材 Sections 2.4–2.5 的全部编号 Example 2.9–2.13。

Prove, for every positive integer \(n\), that
\[
1^2+2^2+\cdots+n^2=\frac16n(n+1)(2n+1).
\]






提示Solution





For \(n=1\),
\[
\text{LHS}=1,
\;
\text{RHS}=\frac16(1)(2)(3)=1.
\]
Assume the result is true for \(n=k\):
\[
1^2+2^2+\cdots+k^2=\frac16k(k+1)(2k+1).
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
1^2+\cdots+k^2+(k+1)^2
&=\frac16k(k+1)(2k+1)+(k+1)^2\\
&=\frac16(k+1)\{k(2k+1)+6(k+1)\}\\
&=\frac16(k+1)(2k^2+7k+6)\\
&=\frac16(k+1)(k+2)(2k+3).
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the required formula with \(n=k+1\). Therefore the implication from \(k\) to \(k+1\) holds. Since the result is true for \(n=1\), it is true for every positive integer \(n\) by mathematical induction.





The sequence is defined by
\[
u_{n+1}=4u_n-3,
\;
u_1=2.
\]
Prove that \(u_n=4^{n-1}+1\).






提示Solution





For \(n=1\), the formula gives \(u_1=4^0+1=2\), so the base case is true.
Assume that for \(n=k\),
\[
u_k=4^{k-1}+1.
\]
Using the recurrence,
\[
\begin{aligned}
u_{k+1}&=4u_k-3\\
&=4(4^{k-1}+1)-3\\
&=4^k+1.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the proposed formula for \(n=k+1\). Hence the result is true for all positive integers \(n\) by mathematical induction.





Prove that \(n!>2^n\) for every integer \(n\ge4\).






提示Solution





For \(n=4\),
\[
4!=24>16=2^4.
\]
Assume that \(k!>2^k\) for some integer \(k\ge4\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
(k+1)!&=(k+1)k!\\
&>(k+1)2^k\\
&>2\cdot2^k\\
&=2^{k+1},
\end{aligned}
\]
because \(k+1>2\). Thus the result for \(k\) implies the result for \(k+1\). Since it is true for \(n=4\), it follows by mathematical induction that \(n!>2^n\) for every integer \(n\ge4\).





Prove that, for every positive integer \(n\),
\[
\frac{d^n}{dx^n}(xe^{ax})=na^{n-1}e^{ax}+a^nxe^{ax},
\]
where \(a\) is constant.






提示Solution





For \(n=1\), the product rule gives
\[
\frac d{dx}(xe^{ax})=e^{ax}+axe^{ax},
\]
which agrees with the formula.
Assume that
\[
\frac{d^k}{dx^k}(xe^{ax})=ka^{k-1}e^{ax}+a^kxe^{ax}.
\]
Differentiate once more:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d^{k+1}}{dx^{k+1}}(xe^{ax})
&=\frac d{dx}\left(ka^{k-1}e^{ax}+a^kxe^{ax}\right)\\
&=ka^ke^{ax}+a^ke^{ax}+a^{k+1}xe^{ax}\\
&=(k+1)a^ke^{ax}+a^{k+1}xe^{ax}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the required expression for \(n=k+1\). The formula therefore holds for every positive integer \(n\) by mathematical induction.





Given
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\3&2\end{pmatrix},
\]
prove that
\[
A^n=\frac14
\begin{pmatrix}
3\cdot5^n+1&5^n-1\\
3\cdot5^n-3&5^n+3
\end{pmatrix}.
\]






提示Solution





For \(n=1\), the right-hand side is
\[
\frac14\begin{pmatrix}16&4\\12&8\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\3&2\end{pmatrix}=A.
\]
Assume the formula holds for \(n=k\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
A^{k+1}
&=A^kA\\
&=\frac14
\begin{pmatrix}
3\cdot5^k+1&5^k-1\\
3\cdot5^k-3&5^k+3
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\3&2\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\frac14
\begin{pmatrix}
15\cdot5^k+1&5\cdot5^k-1\\
15\cdot5^k-3&5\cdot5^k+3
\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\frac14
\begin{pmatrix}
3\cdot5^{k+1}+1&5^{k+1}-1\\
3\cdot5^{k+1}-3&5^{k+1}+3
\end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the target for \(n=k+1\). Hence the formula holds for every positive integer \(n\) by mathematical induction.

text:
3. Cambridge examination questions in the textbook
这里只收录教材 Exercise 中明确标注 Cambridge International AS & A Level Further Mathematics 9231 来源的题目。






注记Exercise 2E, Question 10



It is given that \(u_r=r\cdot r!\) for \(r=1,2,3,\ldots\) and
\[
S_n=u_1+u_2+\cdots+u_n.
\]

Write down the values of \(2!-S_1\), \(3!-S_2\), \(4!-S_3\) and \(5!-S_4\).
Conjecture a formula for \(S_n\).
Prove the formula by mathematical induction for every positive integer \(n\).

Source: 9231 Paper 11 Question 3, October/November 2014.






提示Answer








\[
S_1=1,
\; S_2=1+4=5,
\; S_3=5+18=23,
\; S_4=23+96=119.
\]
Hence
\[
2!-S_1=3!-S_2=4!-S_3=5!-S_4=1.
\]

The conjecture is

\[
\boxed{S_n=(n+1)!-1}.
\]

For \(n=1\), \(S_1=1\) and \(2!-1=1\), so the formula is true.

Assume that for \(n=k\),
\[
S_k=(k+1)!-1.
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_{k+1}
&=S_k+(k+1)(k+1)!\\
&=(k+1)!-1+(k+1)(k+1)!\\
&=(k+1)![1+(k+1)]-1\\
&=(k+2)!-1.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the formula for \(n=k+1\). Therefore \(S_n=(n+1)!-1\) for every positive integer \(n\) by mathematical induction.











注记Exercise 2E, Question 11



It is given that
\[
y=(1+x)^2\ln(1+x).
\]

Find \(d^3y/dx^3\).
Prove by mathematical induction that, for every integer \(n\ge3\),

\[
\frac{d^ny}{dx^n}
=(-1)^{n-1}\frac{2(n-3)!}{(1+x)^{n-2}}.
\]
Source: 9231 Paper 11 Question 5, October/November 2015.






提示Answer






Put \(v=1+x\). Then

\[
y'=2v\ln v+v,
\]
\[
y''=2\ln v+3,
\]
and therefore
\[
\boxed{y'''=\frac2{1+x}}.
\]

The result for \(n=3\) gives

\[
(-1)^2\frac{2(0)!}{1+x}=\frac2{1+x},
\]
which agrees with part (i).
Assume that for some \(k\ge3\),
\[
\frac{d^ky}{dx^k}=(-1)^{k-1}2(k-3)!(1+x)^{-(k-2)}.
\]
Differentiate once:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d^{k+1}y}{dx^{k+1}}
&=(-1)^{k-1}2(k-3)![-(k-2)](1+x)^{-(k-1)}\\
&=(-1)^k\frac{2(k-2)!}{(1+x)^{k-1}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the proposed result with \(n=k+1\). Hence the formula holds for every integer \(n\ge3\) by mathematical induction.











注记Exercise 2E, Question 12



Prove by mathematical induction that, for every positive integer \(n\),
\[
\frac{d^n}{dx^n}(e^x\sin x)
=2^{n/2}e^x\sin\left(x+\frac{n\pi}{4}\right).
\]
Source: 9231 Paper 11 Question 3, October/November 2011.






提示Answer





For \(n=1\),
\[
\frac d{dx}(e^x\sin x)=e^x(\sin x+\cos x)
=\sqrt2e^x\sin\left(x+\frac\pi4\right),
\]
so the formula is true.
Assume that for \(n=k\),
\[
\frac{d^k}{dx^k}(e^x\sin x)
=2^{k/2}e^x\sin\left(x+\frac{k\pi}{4}\right).
\]
Let \(\theta=x+k\pi/4\). Differentiating gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d^{k+1}}{dx^{k+1}}(e^x\sin x)
&=2^{k/2}e^x(\sin\theta+\cos\theta)\\
&=2^{k/2}\sqrt2e^x\sin\left(\theta+\frac\pi4\right)\\
&=2^{(k+1)/2}e^x\sin\left(x+\frac{(k+1)\pi}{4}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the target for \(n=k+1\). Therefore the formula holds for every positive integer \(n\) by mathematical induction.

title: 1.7 Proof by induction
text:
4. Past-paper question bank
完全相同的地区版本合并为一题，并列出全部来源。答案保留 base case、hypothesis、inductive step 与 conclusion。

2019






注记May/June 2019, Paper 11/12, Question 8




Prove by mathematical induction that, for \(z\ne1\) and every positive integer \(n\),

\[
1+z+z^2+\cdots+z^{n-1}=\frac{z^n-1}{z-1}.
\]
[5]

By taking

\[
z=\frac12(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta),
\]
use de Moivre’s theorem to deduce that
\[
\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}2^{-m}\sin(m\theta)
=\frac{2\sin\theta}{5-4\cos\theta}.
\]
[5]
Sources: 9231/11/M/J/19 Q8; 9231/12/M/J/19 Q8.






提示Mark-scheme-style answer






For \(n=1\),

\[
1=\frac{z-1}{z-1}.
\]
Assume that
\[
1+z+\cdots+z^{k-1}=\frac{z^k-1}{z-1}.
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
1+z+\cdots+z^{k-1}+z^k
&=\frac{z^k-1}{z-1}+z^k\\
&=\frac{z^k-1+z^k(z-1)}{z-1}\\
&=\frac{z^{k+1}-1}{z-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the target for \(n=k+1\). Hence the identity holds for every positive integer \(n\) by mathematical induction.

Here \(|z|=1/2<1\), so the infinite geometric series gives

\[
\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}z^m=\frac1{1-z}.
\]
Taking imaginary parts and applying de Moivre’s theorem,
\[
\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}2^{-m}\sin(m\theta)
=\operatorname{Im}\left(\frac1{1-\frac12(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)}\right).
\]
Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate. The denominator is
\[
1-\cos\theta+\frac14
=\frac14(5-4\cos\theta),
\]
and the imaginary part of the numerator is \(\frac12\sin\theta\). Therefore
\[
\boxed{\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}2^{-m}\sin(m\theta)
=\frac{2\sin\theta}{5-4\cos\theta}}.
\]











注记May/June 2019, Paper 13, Question 1



Prove by mathematical induction that \(3^{3n}-1\) is divisible by \(13\) for every positive integer \(n\). [5]
Source: 9231/13/M/J/19 Q1.






提示Mark-scheme-style answer





For \(n=1\),
\[
3^3-1=26=2\cdot13.
\]
Assume that \(3^{3k}-1=13m\) for some integer \(m\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
3^{3(k+1)}-1
&=27\cdot3^{3k}-1\\
&=26\cdot3^{3k}+(3^{3k}-1)\\
&=13(2\cdot3^{3k}+m).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the result holds for \(k+1\), and hence for every positive integer \(n\) by mathematical induction.











注记October/November 2019, Paper 11/12/13, Question 2



It is given that \(y=\ln(ax+1)\), where \(a>0\). Prove by mathematical induction that, for every positive integer \(n\),
\[
\frac{d^ny}{dx^n}
=(-1)^{n-1}\frac{(n-1)!a^n}{(ax+1)^n}.
\]
[6]
Sources: 9231/11/O/N/19 Q2; 9231/12/O/N/19 Q2; 9231/13/O/N/19 Q2.






提示Mark-scheme-style answer





For \(n=1\),
\[
y'=\frac{a}{ax+1},
\]
which agrees with the formula.
Assume that
\[
\frac{d^ky}{dx^k}
=(-1)^{k-1}(k-1)!a^k(ax+1)^{-k}.
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d^{k+1}y}{dx^{k+1}}
&=(-1)^{k-1}(k-1)!a^k(-k)a(ax+1)^{-k-1}\\
&=(-1)^k\frac{k!a^{k+1}}{(ax+1)^{k+1}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the formula for \(n=k+1\). Hence it holds for every positive integer \(n\) by mathematical induction.







2020






注记May/June 2020, Paper 11/12, Question 6



Let
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The transformation represented by \(A^{-1}\) maps a triangle of area \(30\text{ cm}^2\) onto one of area \(d\text{ cm}^2\). Find \(d\). [3]
Prove by mathematical induction that, for every positive integer \(n\),

\[
A^n=\begin{pmatrix}2^n&0\\2^n-1&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
[5]
Sources: 9231/11/M/J/20 Q6; 9231/12/M/J/20 Q6.






提示Mark-scheme-style answer






Since \(\det A=2\),

\[
|\det A^{-1}|=\frac12.
\]
Thus \(\boxed{d=15}\).

For \(n=1\), the proposed expression is \(A\).

Assume that
\[
A^k=\begin{pmatrix}2^k&0\\2^k-1&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
A^{k+1}
&=A^kA\\
&=\begin{pmatrix}2^k&0\\2^k-1&1\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\begin{pmatrix}2^{k+1}&0\\2(2^k-1)+1&1\end{pmatrix}\\
&=\begin{pmatrix}2^{k+1}&0\\2^{k+1}-1&1\end{pmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the formula for \(n=k+1\). Hence it holds for every positive integer \(n\) by mathematical induction.











注记May/June 2020, Paper 13, Question 2



The sequence satisfies \(u_1=1\) and
\[
u_{n+1}=2u_n+1.
\]

Prove by induction that \(u_n=2^n-1\) for every positive integer \(n\). [5]
Deduce that \(u_{2n}\) is divisible by \(u_n\) for \(n\ge1\). [2]

Source: 9231/13/M/J/20 Q2.






提示Mark-scheme-style answer






For \(n=1\), \(2^1-1=1=u_1\).

Assume that \(u_k=2^k-1\). Then
\[
u_{k+1}=2u_k+1=2(2^k-1)+1=2^{k+1}-1.
\]
Thus the result holds for \(k+1\), and hence for every positive integer \(n\) by mathematical induction.



\[
u_{2n}=2^{2n}-1=(2^n-1)(2^n+1)=u_n(2^n+1).
\]
Since \(2^n+1\) is an integer, \(\boxed{u_n\mid u_{2n}}\).











注记October/November 2020, Paper 11/13, Question 5



Prove by mathematical induction that, for every positive integer \(n\),
\[
\frac{d^{2n-1}}{dx^{2n-1}}(x\sin x)
=(-1)^{n-1}\{x\cos x+(2n-1)\sin x\}.
\]
[7]
Sources: 9231/11/O/N/20 Q5; 9231/13/O/N/20 Q5.






提示Mark-scheme-style answer





For \(n=1\),
\[
\frac d{dx}(x\sin x)=x\cos x+\sin x,
\]
which is the proposed expression.
Assume that
\[
\frac{d^{2k-1}}{dx^{2k-1}}(x\sin x)
=(-1)^{k-1}\{x\cos x+(2k-1)\sin x\}.
\]
Differentiate twice. First,
\[
\frac{d^{2k}}{dx^{2k}}(x\sin x)
=(-1)^{k-1}\{-x\sin x+2k\cos x\}.
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d^{2k+1}}{dx^{2k+1}}(x\sin x)
&=(-1)^{k-1}\{-x\cos x-(2k+1)\sin x\}\\
&=(-1)^k\{x\cos x+(2k+1)\sin x\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the target for \(n=k+1\). Hence the formula holds for every positive integer \(n\) by mathematical induction.











注记October/November 2020, Paper 12, Question 2



Prove by mathematical induction that \(7^{2n}-1\) is divisible by \(12\) for every positive integer \(n\). [5]
Source: 9231/12/O/N/20 Q2.






提示Mark-scheme-style answer





For \(n=1\),
\[
7^2-1=48=4\cdot12.
\]
Assume that \(7^{2k}-1=12m\) for some integer \(m\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
7^{2(k+1)}-1
&=49\cdot7^{2k}-1\\
&=49(7^{2k}-1)+48\\
&=12(49m+4).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the expression is divisible by \(12\) for \(n=k+1\). Hence the result follows for every positive integer \(n\) by mathematical induction.







2021






注记May/June 2021, Paper 11/12, Question 1



Prove by mathematical induction that \(2^{4n}+31^n-2\) is divisible by \(15\) for every positive integer \(n\). [6]
Sources: 9231/11/M/J/21 Q1; 9231/12/M/J/21 Q1.






提示Mark-scheme-style answer





For \(n=1\),
\[
2^4+31-2=45=3\cdot15.
\]
Assume that \(2^{4k}+31^k-2=15m\) for some integer \(m\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
2^{4(k+1)}+31^{k+1}-2
&=(15+1)2^{4k}+(30+1)31^k-2\\
&=(2^{4k}+31^k-2)+15\cdot2^{4k}+30\cdot31^k\\
&=15\{m+2^{4k}+2\cdot31^k\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The bracket is an integer. Hence the expression is divisible by \(15\) for \(n=k+1\), and therefore for every positive integer \(n\) by mathematical induction.











注记May/June 2021, Paper 13, Question 3




Prove by mathematical induction that, for every positive integer \(n\),

\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}(5r^4+r^2)
=\frac12n^2(n+1)^2(2n+1).
\]
[6]

Hence, using the standard formula for \(\sum r^2\), find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}r^4\) in fully factorised form. [3]

Source: 9231/13/M/J/21 Q3.






提示Mark-scheme-style answer






For \(n=1\), the left side is \(6\) and the right side is

\[
\frac12(1)^2(2)^2(3)=6.

Assume that
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{k}(5r^4+r^2)
=\frac12k^2(k+1)^2(2k+1).

Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{r=1}^{k+1}(5r^4+r^2)
&=\frac12k^2(k+1)^2(2k+1)+5(k+1)^4+(k+1)^2\\
&=\frac12(k+1)^2\{2k^3+11k^2+20k+12\}\\
&=\frac12(k+1)^2(k+2)^2(2k+3).
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the result for \(n=k+1\). Hence part (a) follows by mathematical induction.



\[
5\sum_{r=1}^{n}r^4+\frac16n(n+1)(2n+1)
=\frac12n^2(n+1)^2(2n+1).

Therefore
\[

&>3\ln a_k\\
&\ge3^k\ln2.

&=3\ln\left(a_n+\frac1{a_n}\right)-\ln a_n\\
&>2\ln a_n\\

It is given that \(y=xe^{ax}\), where \(a\) is constant. Prove by mathematical induction that, for every positive integer \(n\),

\]

提示Mark-scheme-style answer





For \(n=1\),
\[

\frac{d^ky}{dx^k}=(a^kx+ka^{k-1})e^{ax}.

\begin{aligned}
\frac{d^{k+1}y}{dx^{k+1}}
&=a(a^kx+ka^{k-1})e^{ax}+a^ke^{ax}\\
&=\{a^{k+1}x+(k+1)a^k\}e^{ax}.

\]
This is the target for \(n=k+1\). Hence the result holds for every positive integer \(n\) by mathematical induction.

A^k=\begin{pmatrix}1&ka\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.

注记October/November 2023, Paper 11/13, Question 2



For \(x\ne1\), prove by mathematical induction that, for every positive integer \(n\),
\[
1+2x+3x^2+\cdots+nx^{n-1}
=\frac{1-(n+1)x^n+nx^{n+1}}{(1-x)^2}.
\]
[6]
Sources: 9231/11/O/N/23 Q2; 9231/13/O/N/23 Q2.






提示Mark-scheme-style answer





For \(n=1\),
\[
\text{LHS}=1,
\;
\text{RHS}=\frac{1-2x+x^2}{(1-x)^2}=1.
\]
Assume that
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{k}rx^{r-1}
=\frac{1-(k+1)x^k+kx^{k+1}}{(1-x)^2}.
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{r=1}^{k+1}rx^{r-1}
&=\frac{1-(k+1)x^k+kx^{k+1}}{(1-x)^2}+(k+1)x^k\\
&=\frac{1-(k+1)x^k+kx^{k+1}+(k+1)x^k(1-x)^2}{(1-x)^2}\\
&=\frac{1-(k+2)x^{k+1}+(k+1)x^{k+2}}{(1-x)^2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the target for \(n=k+1\). Hence the identity holds for every positive integer \(n\) by mathematical induction.











注记October/November 2023, Paper 12, Question 2



Prove by mathematical induction that, for every positive integer \(n\),
\[
\frac{d^n}{dx^n}(x^2e^x)
=\{x^2+2nx+n(n-1)\}e^x.
\]
[6]
Source: 9231/12/O/N/23 Q2.






提示Mark-scheme-style answer





For \(n=1\),
\[
\frac d{dx}(x^2e^x)=(x^2+2x)e^x,
\]
which agrees with the formula.
Assume that
\[
\frac{d^k}{dx^k}(x^2e^x)
=\{x^2+2kx+k(k-1)\}e^x.
\]
Differentiate once:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d^{k+1}}{dx^{k+1}}(x^2e^x)
&=\{x^2+2kx+k(k-1)+2x+2k\}e^x\\
&=\{x^2+2(k+1)x+k(k+1)\}e^x.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the proposed formula for \(n=k+1\). Hence it holds for every positive integer \(n\) by mathematical induction.

Prove by mathematical induction that

6^{4n}+38^n-2

is divisible by \(74\) for every positive integer \(n\). [6]
Sources: 9231/11/M/J/24 Q2; 9231/12/M/J/24 Q2.

\[
6^4+38-2=1332=18\cdot74.

Assume that
\[
6^{4k}+38^k-2=74m
\]
for some integer \(m\). Then

\begin{aligned}
6^{4(k+1)}+38^{k+1}-2
&=1296\cdot6^{4k}+38\cdot38^k-2\\
&=1296(6^{4k}+38^k-2)-1258\cdot38^k+2590\\
&=74\{1296m-17\cdot38^k+35\}.

注记May/June 2024, Paper 13, Question 4




Prove by mathematical induction that, for every positive integer \(n\),

\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}r^2=\frac16n(n+1)(2n+1).
\]
[5]
The sum \(S_n\) is defined by \(S_n=\sum_{r=1}^{n}r^4\).

Using

\[
(2r+1)^5-(2r-1)^5=160r^4+80r^2+2,
\]
show that
\[
S_n=\frac1{30}n(n+1)(2n+1)(3n^2+3n-1).
\]
[6]
Source: 9231/13/M/J/24 Q4.






提示Mark-scheme-style answer






For \(n=1\), both sides equal \(1\).

Assume
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{k}r^2=\frac16k(k+1)(2k+1).
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{r=1}^{k+1}r^2
&=\frac16k(k+1)(2k+1)+(k+1)^2\\
&=\frac16(k+1)(2k^2+7k+6)\\
&=\frac16(k+1)(k+2)(2k+3).
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the result for \(n=k+1\). Therefore the formula holds for every positive integer \(n\) by mathematical induction.

Sum the given identity from \(r=1\) to \(r=n\). The left side telescopes:

\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}\{(2r+1)^5-(2r-1)^5\}=(2n+1)^5-1.
\]
Hence
\[
(2n+1)^5-1=160S_n+80\sum_{r=1}^{n}r^2+2n.
\]
Using part (a),
\[
160S_n=(2n+1)^5-1-\frac{40}{3}n(n+1)(2n+1)-2n.
\]

\boxed{S_n=\frac1{30}n(n+1)(2n+1)(3n^2+3n-1)}.

注记October/November 2024, Paper 11/13, Question 2



Prove by mathematical induction that, for every positive integer \(n\),
\[
\frac{d^n}{dx^n}(\tan^{-1}x)=P_n(x)(1+x^2)^{-n},
\]
where \(P_n(x)\) is a polynomial of degree \(n-1\). [6]
Sources: 9231/11/O/N/24 Q2; 9231/13/O/N/24 Q2.






提示Mark-scheme-style answer





For \(n=1\),
\[
\frac d{dx}(\tan^{-1}x)=(1+x^2)^{-1}.
\]
Thus \(P_1(x)=1\), which has degree \(0=1-1\).
Assume that
\[
\frac{d^k}{dx^k}(\tan^{-1}x)=P_k(x)(1+x^2)^{-k},
\]
where \(P_k\) has degree \(k-1\). Differentiating,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d^{k+1}}{dx^{k+1}}(\tan^{-1}x)
&=P_k'(x)(1+x^2)^{-k}-2kxP_k(x)(1+x^2)^{-k-1}\\
&=\{(1+x^2)P_k'(x)-2kxP_k(x)\}(1+x^2)^{-k-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Define
\[
P_{k+1}(x)=(1+x^2)P_k'(x)-2kxP_k(x).
\]
Both terms have degree at most \(k\), and the leading coefficient is non-zero, so \(P_{k+1}\) has degree \(k\). This is the required form for \(n=k+1\). Hence the result follows for every positive integer \(n\) by mathematical induction.

Prove by induction that \(u_n=3^n+1\) for every positive integer \(n\). [5]

u_{k+1}&=3u_k-2\\

Prove by mathematical induction that, for every integer \(n\ge2\),
\[
\frac{d^n}{dx^n}(x\ln x)=(-1)^n(n-2)!x^{1-n}.

[6]

\;
\frac{d^2}{dx^2}(x\ln x)=\frac1x.
\]
The proposed expression gives \((-1)^2(0)!x^{-1}=1/x\), so the base case holds.

&=(-1)^k(k-2)!(1-k)x^{-k}\\

注记October/November 2025, Paper 11/13, Question 3



Prove by mathematical induction that, for every positive integer \(n\),
\[
\frac{d^{2n-1}}{dx^{2n-1}}(x\cos x)

提示Mark-scheme-style answer

=(-1)\{x\sin x-\cos x\}.

Assume that for \(n=k\),

=(-1)^k\{x\sin x-(2k-1)\cos x\}.

(-1)^k\{x\cos x+2k\sin x\}.

&=(-1)^{k+1}\{x\sin x-(2k+1)\cos x\}.

title: 1.5 Polar coordinates
text:
学习路线


能在 Cartesian coordinates 与 principal polar coordinates 之间转换
能把直线、圆和简单代数曲线的方程转换为极坐标形式或 Cartesian 形式

title: 1.5 Polar coordinates
text:
1. 教材知识点

1.1 Polar coordinates of a point
点 \(P\) 的极坐标写成 \((r,\theta)\)：\(r\) 是 \(P\) 到 pole \(O\) 的距离，\(\theta\) 是从 initial line 逆时针量到 \(OP\) 的角，通常用弧度表示。
同一点有无限多种表示：
\[
(r,\theta)\equiv(r,\theta+2k\pi),\; k\in\mathbb Z.
\]
本教材的 principal polar coordinates 满足
\[
r>0,\; -\pi<\theta\leqslant\pi.
\]
在 pole 处 \(r=0\)，而 \(\theta\) 没有唯一值。


1.2 Converting points and equations
两种坐标之间的基本关系是
\[
x=r\cos\theta,\; y=r\sin\theta,
\; r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2},\; \tan\theta=\frac yx.
\]
由 Cartesian coordinates 求 \(\theta\) 时，必须结合点所在象限选择正确的角，不能只使用计算器给出的 \(\arctan(y/x)\)。
转换曲线方程时常用
\[
r^2=x^2+y^2,\; r\cos\theta=x,\; r\sin\theta=y.
\]
如果极坐标式中仍含 \(\sin\theta\) 或 \(\cos\theta\)，可乘以适当的 \(r\) 的幂，使它们与 \(x\)、\(y\) 配对。平方消去根号时，应保留原极坐标方程所给的 \(r\) 与 \(\theta\) 范围。


1.3 Sketching a polar curve
作图时依次检查：

Range of \(\theta\) and the convention \(r\geqslant0\)：先确定题目要求的角度范围，再排除使 \(r<0\) 的部分；
Pole：解 \(r=0\)，确定曲线从哪些方向到达或离开 pole；
Initial line：检查 \(\theta=0\)，以及区间内与 initial line 同方向的角；
Symmetry：比较 \(r(-\theta)\)、\(r(\pi-\theta)\) 或观察函数的周期；
Least and greatest values of \(r\)：由三角函数范围或微分求极值；
Direction and shape：取少量关键角，按 \(\theta\) 增大的方向连接。







注记Convention used in this course



若公式给出 \(r<0\)，本课程不把点画到相反方向，也不以虚线延伸；只绘制 \(r\geqslant0\) 的部分。




1.4 Symmetry tests
以下代换可帮助判断对称性：
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{test} & \text{possible symmetry}\\ \hline
\theta\mapsto-\theta & \text{initial line}\\
\theta\mapsto\pi-\theta & \theta=\frac\pi2\\
\theta\mapsto\theta+\pi & \text{pole}
\end{array}
\]
即使方程形式在代换后不完全相同，也可根据给定区间、周期和关键点确认实际图形的对称性。


1.5 Distances from lines
点 \((r,\theta)\) 到 initial line 的垂直距离为
\[
|y|=|r\sin\theta|.
\]
在第一象限内可直接使用 \(r\sin\theta\)。点到半直线 \(\theta=\alpha\) 所在直线的垂直距离为
\[
|r\sin(\theta-\alpha)|.
\]
求最远点时，应对相应距离函数微分，并检查端点以及区间内部的 stationary points。


1.6 Intersections of polar curves
在共同的 \(\theta\) 范围内令两个 \(r\) 表达式相等。还必须单独检查 pole，因为不同的 \(\theta\) 值都可能表示 \(r=0\) 的同一点。
若一条曲线是直线 \(r\sin\theta=c\)，它的 Cartesian equation 是 \(y=c\)；这有时能帮助判断交点个数和位置。


1.7 Area enclosed by a polar curve
曲线 \(r=f(\theta)\)、半直线 \(\theta=\alpha\) 与 \(\theta=\beta\) 所围区域的面积为
\[
\boxed{A=\frac12\int_\alpha^\beta r^2\,\mathrm d\theta}.
\]
选择上下限前，应先由 \(r=0\)、曲线交点或题目给出的半直线确定边界。若图形关于某条直线对称，可只积一半再乘以 \(2\)。
两条曲线之间的面积通常写成
\[
A=\frac12\int_\alpha^\beta
\left(r_{\text{outer}}^2-r_{\text{inner}}^2\right)\,\mathrm d\theta.
\]

title: 1.5 Polar coordinates
text:
2. Textbook Examples

Example 5.1 · Pages 118–119
(i) Find the Cartesian coordinates of:
\[
\left(4,\frac{2\pi}{3}\right),\;
\left(12,-\frac\pi6\right).
\]
(ii) Find the principal polar coordinates of:
\[
(-\sqrt3,1),\; (4,-4).
\]


Show solution

(i) Using \(x=r\cos\theta\) and \(y=r\sin\theta\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
x&=4\cos\frac{2\pi}{3}=-2,&
y&=4\sin\frac{2\pi}{3}=2\sqrt3,\\
x&=12\cos\left(-\frac\pi6\right)=6\sqrt3,&
y&=12\sin\left(-\frac\pi6\right)=-6.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence the Cartesian coordinates are
\[
\boxed{(-2,2\sqrt3)},\;
\boxed{(6\sqrt3,-6)}.
\]
(ii) For \((-\sqrt3,1)\),
\[
r=\sqrt{(-\sqrt3)^2+1^2}=2.
\]
The point is in quadrant II and its reference angle is \(\pi/6\), so
\[
\boxed{\left(2,\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)}.
\]
For \((4,-4)\),
\[
r=\sqrt{4^2+(-4)^2}=4\sqrt2.
\]
The point is in quadrant IV, so the principal angle is \(-\pi/4\). Thus
\[
\boxed{\left(4\sqrt2,-\frac\pi4\right)}.
\]



Example 5.1: points in polar and Cartesian form

Each point is located by a radius from the pole and an angle from the initial line.   Example 5.1: points in polar and Cartesian form initial lineyO(4, 2π/3)(12, −π/6)(−√3, 1)(4, −4)


Each point is located by a radius from the pole and an angle from the initial line.



 Completed


Example 5.2 · Pages 120–121
Find polar equations of the curves
\[
\text{(i) }x^2-y^2=9,\;
\text{(ii) }y=x+4.
\]


Show solution

(i) Substitute \(x=r\cos\theta\) and \(y=r\sin\theta\):
\[
r^2(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta)=9.
\]
Since \(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta=\cos2\theta\),
\[
\boxed{r^2=9\sec2\theta}.
\]
(ii) Substitution gives
\[
r\sin\theta=r\cos\theta+4,
\]
so
\[
r(\sin\theta-\cos\theta)=4.
\]
Using
\[
\sin\theta-\cos\theta
=\sqrt2\sin\left(\theta-\frac\pi4\right),
\]
the required equation is
\[
\boxed{r=2\sqrt2\,\cosec\left(\theta-\frac\pi4\right)}.
\]



Example 5.2: Cartesian curves before conversion

The same geometric curves can be described by polar equations.   Example 5.2: Cartesian curves before conversion initial lineyOx² − y² = 9y = x + 4


The same geometric curves can be described by polar equations.



 Completed


Example 5.3 · Page 121
Find Cartesian equations of the curves
\[
\text{(i) }r=5,\;
\text{(ii) }r^2=4\sin\theta.
\]


Show solution

(i) Since \(r^2=x^2+y^2\),
\[
\boxed{x^2+y^2=25}.
\]
(ii) Multiply by \(r\):
\[
r^3=4r\sin\theta=4y.
\]
Squaring and using \(r^2=x^2+y^2\) gives
\[
r^6=16y^2,
\]
and hence
\[
\boxed{(x^2+y^2)^3=16y^2}.
\]



Example 5.3: r = 5 and r² = 4 sin θ

The plotted polar curves correspond to the derived Cartesian equations.   Example 5.3: r = 5 and r² = 4 sin θ initial lineyO-55r = 5r² = 4 sin θ


The plotted polar curves correspond to the derived Cartesian equations.



 Completed


Example 5.4 · Page 124
Sketch the graphs of
\[
\text{(i) }r=3,\;
\text{(ii) }\theta=\frac\pi4.
\]


Show solution

For \(r=3\), every point is a distance \(3\) from the pole, so the graph is a circle with centre \(O\) and radius \(3\). It crosses the initial line at \((3,0)\).
For \(\theta=\pi/4\), the angle is fixed while \(r\geqslant0\) varies. The graph is therefore a half-line from the pole at angle \(\pi/4\); it is not the complete Cartesian line \(y=x\).



Example 5.4: a constant radius and a constant angle

A constant r gives a circle; a constant θ gives a half-line.   Example 5.4: a constant radius and a constant angle initial lineyO-33r = 3θ = π/4(3, 0)


A constant r gives a circle; a constant θ gives a half-line.



 Completed


Example 5.5 · Page 125
A curve is defined by
\[
r=5\cos^2\theta.
\]
(i) Create a table of values for \(0\leqslant\theta\leqslant\pi\).
(ii) Plot the curve for \(0\leqslant\theta\leqslant2\pi\).
(iii) State the least and greatest values of \(r\) and the values of \(\theta\) at which they occur.


Show solution

At intervals of \(\pi/12\) from \(0\) to \(\pi/2\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrr}
\theta&0&\frac\pi{12}&\frac\pi6&\frac\pi4&\frac\pi3&\frac{5\pi}{12}&\frac\pi2\\ \hline
r&5&4.67&3.75&2.50&1.25&0.34&0
\end{array}
\]
The values are reflected between \(\pi/2\) and \(\pi\) and repeat with period \(\pi\). The initial line is an axis of symmetry.
Since \(0\leqslant\cos^2\theta\leqslant1\),
\[
\boxed{r_{\max}=5\text{ at }\theta=0,\pi},
\]
and
\[
\boxed{r_{\min}=0\text{ at }\theta=\frac\pi2,\frac{3\pi}{2}}.
\]



Example 5.5: r = 5 cos² θ

The curve is symmetric about both coordinate axes and reaches the pole when cos θ = 0.   Example 5.5: r = 5 cos² θ initial lineyO-55r = 5r = 5


The curve is symmetric about both coordinate axes and reaches the pole when cos θ = 0.



 Completed


Example 5.6 · Page 126
Find the least and greatest values of \(r\) for
\[
r=3+2\cos4\theta
\]
and the values of \(\theta\) at which they occur. Hence sketch the graph.


Show solution

The least value is
\[
3-2=1,
\]
which occurs when \(\cos4\theta=-1\). For \(-\pi<\theta\leqslant\pi\), this gives
\[
\theta=\pm\frac\pi4,\ \pm\frac{3\pi}{4}.
\]
The greatest value is
\[
3+2=5,
\]
which occurs when \(\cos4\theta=1\), including
\[
\theta=0,\ \pm\frac\pi2,\ \pi.
\]
The function has period \(\pi/2\), so the graph repeats in each quadrant and has rotational symmetry of order \(4\). It never reaches the pole because \(r\geqslant1\).



Example 5.6: r = 3 + 2 cos 4θ

Fourfold rotational symmetry; 1 ≤ r ≤ 5.   Example 5.6: r = 3 + 2 cos 4θ initial lineyO-11-55


Fourfold rotational symmetry; 1 ≤ r ≤ 5.



 Completed


Example 5.7 · Pages 126–129
A curve is given by
\[
r=\theta(\pi-\theta).
\]
(i) Plot the curve for \(0\leqslant\theta\leqslant\pi\), where \(r\) is non-negative.
(ii) Create tables of values for \(\pi\leqslant\theta\leqslant3\pi/2\) and \(-\pi/2\leqslant\theta\leqslant0\).
(iii) Sketch the curve for \(-\pi/2\leqslant\theta\leqslant3\pi/2\) using the convention for this course.


Show solution

For \(0\leqslant\theta\leqslant\pi\), \(r\geqslant0\). The curve starts at the pole when \(\theta=0\), reaches its greatest radius at \(\theta=\pi/2\), and returns to the pole at \(\theta=\pi\):
\[
r_{\max}=\frac\pi2\left(\pi-\frac\pi2\right)=\frac{\pi^2}{4}.
\]
Outside this interval, \(\theta(\pi-\theta)<0\). For instance,
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrr}
\theta&\pi&\frac{7\pi}{6}&\frac{4\pi}{3}&\frac{3\pi}{2}\\ \hline
r&0&-\frac{7\pi^2}{36}&-\frac{4\pi^2}{9}&-\frac{3\pi^2}{4}
\end{array}
\]
and
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrr}
\theta&-\frac\pi2&-\frac\pi3&-\frac\pi6&0\\ \hline
r&-\frac{3\pi^2}{4}&-\frac{4\pi^2}{9}&-\frac{7\pi^2}{36}&0.
\end{array}
\]
Under the convention \(r\geqslant0\), these negative-radius portions are omitted. The required graph therefore consists only of the loop traced for \(0\leqslant\theta\leqslant\pi\).



Example 5.7: r = θ(π − θ), r ≥ 0

Only the interval 0 ≤ θ ≤ π is drawn because the stated course convention excludes negative r.   Example 5.7: r = θ(π − θ), r ≥ 0 initial lineyOr = π²/4


Only the interval 0 ≤ θ ≤ π is drawn because the stated course convention excludes negative r.



 Completed


Example 5.8 · Pages 132–133
The curve has equation
\[
r=1+2\cos\theta.
\]
Find the area enclosed, using the convention \(r\geqslant0\).


Show solution

The curve reaches the pole when
\[
1+2\cos\theta=0
\Longrightarrow
\cos\theta=-\frac12.
\]
The relevant limiting angles are \(\theta=\pm2\pi/3\). By symmetry about the initial line,
\[
A=2\left(\frac12\int_0^{2\pi/3}(1+2\cos\theta)^2\,\mathrm d\theta\right).
\]
Using \(4\cos^2\theta=2+2\cos2\theta\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
A
&=\int_0^{2\pi/3}(3+4\cos\theta+2\cos2\theta)\,\mathrm d\theta\\
&=\left[3\theta+4\sin\theta+\sin2\theta\right]_0^{2\pi/3}\\
&=2\pi+2\sqrt3-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{A=2\pi+\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}}.
\]



Example 5.8: r = 1 + 2 cos θ

The curve reaches the pole at θ = ±2π/3 and is symmetric about the initial line.   Example 5.8: r = 1 + 2 cos θ initial lineyO-11-33θ = 2π/3θ = −2π/3(3, 0)


The curve reaches the pole at θ = ±2π/3 and is symmetric about the initial line.



 Completed

Exercise 5B · Question 9 · Page 131
The curves \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) have polar equations
\[
C_1:r=\frac12,\; 0\leqslant\theta\leqslant2\pi,
\]
and
\[
C_2:r=\sin\frac\theta2,\; 0\leqslant\theta\leqslant\pi.
\]
Find the polar coordinates of the point of intersection of \(C_1\) and \(C_2\). Sketch \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) on the same diagram.


Show solution

At an intersection away from the pole, the two curves have the same \(r\) and \(\theta\):
\[
\sin\frac\theta2=\frac12.
\]
Since \(0\leqslant\theta/2\leqslant\pi/2\),
\[
\frac\theta2=\frac\pi6
\Longrightarrow
\theta=\frac\pi3.
\]
Thus the point of intersection is
\[
\boxed{\left(\frac12,\frac\pi3\right)}.
\]
\(C_1\) is the circle with centre at the pole and radius \(1/2\). The curve \(C_2\) starts at the pole, passes through the stated intersection and reaches \((-1,0)\) when \(\theta=\pi\).



Exercise 5B Q9: two polar curves

The circle and C₂ meet at θ = π/3.   Exercise 5B Q9: two polar curves initial lineyOC₁: r = 1/2C₂: r = sin(θ/2)(1/2, π/3)


The circle and C₂ meet at θ = π/3.



 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2015, Q5 (part question).





Exercise 5C · Question 9 · Page 134
The curve \(C\) has polar equation
\[
r=a(1+\sin\theta),\; 0\leqslant\theta<2\pi,
\]
where \(a\) is a positive constant. Draw a sketch of \(C\).
Find the exact area of the region enclosed by \(C\) and the half-lines \(\theta=\pi/3\) and \(\theta=2\pi/3\).


Show solution

The curve is symmetric about \(\theta=\pi/2\). It has
\[
r=2a\text{ at }\theta=\frac\pi2,\;
r=0\text{ at }\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2},
\]
and meets the initial line at \(r=a\).
The required area is
\[
A=\frac12a^2\int_{\pi/3}^{2\pi/3}(1+\sin\theta)^2\,\mathrm d\theta.
\]
Since
\[
(1+\sin\theta)^2
=\frac32+2\sin\theta-\frac12\cos2\theta,
\]
we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
A
&=\frac{a^2}{2}
\left[
\frac32\theta-2\cos\theta-\frac14\sin2\theta
\right]_{\pi/3}^{2\pi/3}\\
&=\frac{a^2}{2}left(\frac\pi2+2+\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{A=\frac{a^2}{8}\left(2\pi+8+\sqrt3\right)}.
\]



Exercise 5C Q9: r = a(1 + sin θ)

The required sector lies between the two coral half-lines; the drawing is scaled with a = 1.   Exercise 5C Q9: r = a(1 + sin θ) initial lineyOθ = π/3θ = 2π/3r = 2a


The required sector lies between the two coral half-lines; the drawing is scaled with a = 1.



 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2014, Q5.





Exercise 5C · Question 10 · Page 134
The curve \(C\) has polar equation
\[
r=2+2\cos\theta,\; 0\leqslant\theta<\pi.
\]
Sketch \(C\). Find the area of the region \(R\) enclosed by \(C\) and the initial line.
The half-line \(\theta=\pi/5\) divides \(R\) into two parts. Find the area of each part, correct to \(3\) decimal places.


Show solution

The curve starts at \((4,0)\) and reaches the pole at \(\theta=\pi\). The required region is the part above the initial line.
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{area}(R)
&=\frac12\int_0^\pi(2+2\cos\theta)^2\,\mathrm d\theta\\
&=\int_0^\pi(3+4\cos\theta+\cos2\theta)\,\mathrm d\theta\\
&=\left[3\theta+4\sin\theta+\frac12\sin2\theta\right]_0^\pi\\
&=\boxed{3\pi}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The area between \(\theta=0\) and \(\theta=\pi/5\) is
\[
\begin{aligned}
A_1
&=\left[3\theta+4\sin\theta+\frac12\sin2\theta\right]_0^{\pi/5}\\
&=4.71163\ldots\\
&=\boxed{4.712}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The remaining area is
\[
A_2=3\pi-A_1=4.71315\ldots=\boxed{4.713}.
\]



Exercise 5C Q10: r = 2 + 2 cos θ

The half-line θ = π/5 divides the upper half-cardioid into the two required regions.   Exercise 5C Q10: r = 2 + 2 cos θ initial lineyO-44θ = π/5(4, 0)


The half-line θ = π/5 divides the upper half-cardioid into the two required regions.



 Completed

4. Past-paper question bank






注记



以下题目按完全相同的地区版本合并，所有图形均由题目中的极坐标方程重新绘制，答案依据对应的 Cambridge mark scheme 展开。



2019



2019 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 11 EITHER · 14 marks
\(C_1\) has equation \(r^2=2\theta\) for \(0\leqslant\theta\leqslant\pi/2\). The point \(P\) is furthest from the line \(\theta=\pi/2\).
(i) Show that \(2\theta\tan\theta=1\) at \(P\), and verify a root between \(0.6\) and \(0.7\). [5]
\(C_2\) has equation \(r^2=\theta\sec^2\theta\) for \(0\leqslant\theta<\pi/2\). The curves meet at the pole and at \(Q\).
(ii) Find the exact value of \(\theta\) at \(Q\). [2]
(iii) Sketch \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) together. [2]
(iv) Find exactly the area enclosed by the curves. [5]


Show answer and mark scheme

(i) Distance from \(\theta=\pi/2\) is \(x=r\cos\theta=(2\theta)^{1/2}\cos\theta\). Hence
\[
\frac{dx}{d\theta}=(2\theta)^{1/2}\left(\frac{\cos\theta}{2\theta}-\sin\theta\right)=0
\Longrightarrow \boxed{2\theta\tan\theta=1}.
\]
For \(f(\theta)=2\theta\tan\theta-1\),
\[f(0.6)=-0.179<0,\; f(0.7)=0.179>0,\]
so a root lies in \((0.6,0.7)\).
(ii) Away from the pole,
\[2\theta=\theta\sec^2\theta\Longrightarrow\cos^2\theta=\frac12,\]
so \(\boxed{\theta=\pi/4}\).
(iv) \(C_1\) is outside \(C_2\) for \(0<\theta<\pi/4\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
A&=\frac12\int_0^{\pi/4}\left(2\theta-\theta\sec^2\theta\right)d\theta\\
&=\boxed{\frac{\pi^2}{32}-\frac\pi8+\frac14\ln2}.
\end{aligned}
\]



2019 M/J 11–12: C₁ and C₂

The curves meet at θ = π/4; the shaded-area calculation uses 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/4.   2019 M/J 11–12: C₁ and C₂ initial lineyOC₁C₂Q


The curves meet at θ = π/4; the shaded-area calculation uses 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/4.




Sources: 9231/11/M/J/2019 Q11 EITHER; 9231/12/M/J/2019 Q11 EITHER.





2019 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 2 · 7 marks
\(C\) has equation \(r^2=\ln(1+\theta)\) for \(0\leqslant\theta\leqslant2\pi\).
(i) Sketch \(C\). [2]
(ii) Find exactly the area bounded by \(C\) and the initial line. [5]


Show answer and mark scheme

The curve starts at the pole, spirals anticlockwise with increasing \(r\), and returns to the initial line at \(\theta=2\pi\); it is tangent to the initial line at the pole.
\[
\begin{aligned}
A&=\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}\ln(1+\theta)d\theta\\
&=\frac12\int_1^{2\pi+1}\ln u\,du\\
&=\frac12[u\ln u-u]_1^{2\pi+1}\\
&=\boxed{\left(\pi+\frac12\right)\ln(2\pi+1)-\pi}.
\end{aligned}
\]



2019 M/J 13: r² = ln(1 + θ)

An increasing anticlockwise spiral, tangent to the initial line at the pole.   2019 M/J 13: r² = ln(1 + θ) initial lineyO


An increasing anticlockwise spiral, tangent to the initial line at the pole.




Source: 9231/13/M/J/2019 Q2.





2019 October/November · 9231/11, /12 & /13 · Question 11 EITHER · 14 marks
For \(0\leqslant\theta\leqslant\pi/2\),
\[C_1:r=2(e^\theta+e^{-\theta}),\; C_2:r=e^{2\theta}-e^{-2\theta}.\]
The curves meet at \(P\) where \(\theta=\alpha\).
(i) Show that \(e^{2\alpha}-2e^\alpha-1=0\), find \(\alpha\) exactly and show that \(r=4\sqrt2\) at \(P\). [6]
(ii) Sketch both curves. [3]
(iii) Find to \(3\) significant figures the area enclosed by the curves and initial line. [5]


Show answer and mark scheme

Equating radii and dividing by \(e^\alpha+e^{-\alpha}\) gives \(e^\alpha-e^{-\alpha}=2\), hence
\[e^{2\alpha}-2e^\alpha-1=0,\; e^\alpha=1+\sqrt2,\]
so
\[\boxed{\alpha=\ln(1+\sqrt2)},\; \boxed{r=4\sqrt2}.\]
The required area is
\[
\frac12\int_0^\alpha\left[4(e^\theta+e^{-\theta})^2-(e^{2\theta}-e^{-2\theta})^2\right]d\theta.
\]
After expansion this equals
\[
\left[5\theta+e^{2\theta}-e^{-2\theta}-\frac18e^{4\theta}+\frac18e^{-4\theta}\right]_0^\alpha
=5\alpha+\sqrt2.
\]
Thus \(\boxed{A=5.82}\) to \(3\) significant figures.



2019 O/N: exponential polar curves

The curves and the initial line enclose the required region before P.   2019 O/N: exponential polar curves initial lineyOC₁C₂P


The curves and the initial line enclose the required region before P.




Sources: 9231/11/O/N/2019 Q11 EITHER; 9231/12/O/N/2019 Q11 EITHER; 9231/13/O/N/2019 Q11 EITHER.




2020



2020 May/June · 9231/11 & /12 · Question 7 · 12 marks
\(C_1:r=\theta\cos\theta\) and \(C_2:r=\theta\sin\theta\), for \(0\leqslant\theta\leqslant\pi/2\).
(a) Show that the point of \(C_1\) furthest from \(\theta=\pi/2\) satisfies \(2\theta\tan\theta-1=0\), and verify a root in \((0.6,0.7)\). [5]
(b) Find the non-pole intersection. [2] (c) Sketch both curves. [3] (d) Find the enclosed area exactly. [2]


Show answer and mark scheme

\(x=r\cos\theta=\theta\cos^2\theta\), so
\[\frac{dx}{d\theta}=\cos^2\theta-2\theta\sin\theta\cos\theta=0
\Longrightarrow 2\theta\tan\theta-1=0.\]
The values at \(0.6\) and \(0.7\) are \(-0.179\) and \(0.179\), establishing the root. At the other intersection,
\[\theta\cos\theta=\theta\sin\theta\Longrightarrow\boxed{(r,\theta)=\left(\frac\pi{4\sqrt2},\frac\pi4\right)}.\]
Finally,
\[
A=\frac12\int_0^{\pi/4}\theta^2(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta)d\theta
=\boxed{\frac{\pi^2}{64}-\frac18}.
\]



2020 M/J 11–12: C₁ and C₂

The curves meet away from the pole at θ = π/4.   2020 M/J 11–12: C₁ and C₂ initial lineyOC₁C₂Q


The curves meet away from the pole at θ = π/4.




Sources: 9231/11/M/J/2020 Q7; 9231/12/M/J/2020 Q7.





2020 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 5 · 6 marks
\(C:r=a\tan\theta\), where \(a>0\) and \(0\leqslant\theta\leqslant\pi/4\).
(a) Sketch \(C\) and state the greatest distance from the pole. [2]
(b) Find exactly the area bounded by \(C\) and \(\theta=\pi/4\). [4]


Show answer and mark scheme

\(r\) increases from \(0\) to \(a\), so the greatest distance is \(\boxed{a}\).
\[
A=\frac{a^2}{2}\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan^2\theta\,d\theta
=\frac{a^2}{2}[\tan\theta-\theta]_0^{\pi/4}
=\boxed{\frac{a^2}{2}\left(1-\frac\pi4\right)}.
\]



2020 M/J 13: r = a tan θ

Scaled with a = 1; the greatest radius is a.   2020 M/J 13: r = a tan θ initial lineyOθ = π/4


Scaled with a = 1; the greatest radius is a.




Source: 9231/13/M/J/2020 Q5.





2020 October/November · 9231/11 & /13 · Question 7 · 11 marks
(a) Show that \((x^2+y^2)^{5/2}=4xy(x^2-y^2)\) has polar equation \(r=\sin4\theta\). [4]
For \(0\leqslant\theta\leqslant\pi/4\), (b) sketch the curve and state its symmetry line; [3] (c) find its enclosed area exactly. [4]


Show answer and mark scheme

Substitution gives
\[r^5=4r^4\cos\theta\sin\theta(\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta),\]
so \(r=2\sin2\theta\cos2\theta=\boxed{\sin4\theta}\). The single loop is symmetric about \(\boxed{\theta=\pi/8}\).
\[A=\frac12\int_0^{\pi/4}\sin^24\theta\,d\theta
=\frac14\left[\theta-\frac18\sin8\theta\right]_0^{\pi/4}
=\boxed{\frac\pi{16}}.\]



2020 O/N 11–13: r = sin 4θ

A single loop symmetric about θ = π/8.   2020 O/N 11–13: r = sin 4θ initial lineyOθ = π/8


A single loop symmetric about θ = π/8.




Sources: 9231/11/O/N/2020 Q7; 9231/13/O/N/2020 Q7.





2020 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 5 · 8 marks
\(C:r=\ln(1+\pi-\theta)\) for \(0\leqslant\theta\leqslant\pi\).
(a) Sketch \(C\) and state the point furthest from the pole. [3]
(b) Find exactly the area bounded by \(C\) and the initial line. [5]


Show answer and mark scheme

\(r\) decreases from \(\ln(1+\pi)\) to \(0\), so the furthest point is \(\boxed{(\ln(1+\pi),0)}\).
With \(u=1+\pi-\theta\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
A&=\frac12\int_1^{1+\pi}\ln^2u\,du\\
&=\frac12[u(\ln^2u-2\ln u+2)]_1^{1+\pi}\\
&=\boxed{\frac12(1+\pi)\{\ln^2(1+\pi)-2\ln(1+\pi)+2\}-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]



2020 O/N 12: r = ln(1 + π − θ)

The radius decreases from ln(1 + π) to zero.   2020 O/N 12: r = ln(1 + π − θ) initial lineyO


The radius decreases from ln(1 + π) to zero.




Source: 9231/12/O/N/2020 Q5.




2021



2021 May/June · 9231/11 & /12 · Question 5 · 7 marks
\(C:r=a\cot(\pi/3-\theta)\), where \(a>0\), \(0\leqslant\theta\leqslant\pi/6\), and the greatest radius is \(2\sqrt3\).
(a) Sketch \(C\) and show that \(a=2\). [3] (b) Find the bounded area exactly. [4]


Show answer and mark scheme

At \(\theta=\pi/6\), \(r=a\cot(\pi/6)=a\sqrt3=2\sqrt3\), hence \(\boxed{a=2}\).
\[
\begin{aligned}
A&=2\int_0^{\pi/6}\cot^2(\pi/3-\theta)d\theta\\
&=2[-\cot u-u]_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3}
=\boxed{\frac{4\sqrt3-\pi}{3}}.
\end{aligned}
\]



2021 M/J 11–12: r = 2 cot(π/3 − θ)

The radius increases to 2√3.   2021 M/J 11–12: r = 2 cot(π/3 − θ) initial lineyOθ = π/6


The radius increases to 2√3.




Sources: 9231/11/M/J/2021 Q5; 9231/12/M/J/2021 Q5.





2021 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 5 · 9 marks
For \(0\leqslant\theta\leqslant\pi/2\),
\[r=\frac1{\pi-\theta}-\frac1\pi.\]
(a) Sketch \(C\). [3] (b) Show that the area bounded by \(C\) and \(\theta=\pi/2\) is \((3-4\ln2)/(4\pi)\). [6]


Show answer and mark scheme

\(r\) increases from \(0\) and the curve is tangent to the initial line at the pole.
\[
A=\frac1{2\pi^2}\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\theta^2}{(\pi-\theta)^2}d\theta.
\]
Let \(u=\pi-\theta\). Then
\[A=\frac1{2\pi^2}\int_{\pi/2}^{\pi}\left(\frac{\pi^2}{u^2}-\frac{2\pi}{u}+1\right)du
=\boxed{\frac{3-4\ln2}{4\pi}}.\]



2021 M/J 13: reciprocal-difference curve

The curve leaves the pole tangentially and has increasing radius.   2021 M/J 13: reciprocal-difference curve initial lineyO


The curve leaves the pole tangentially and has increasing radius.




Source: 9231/13/M/J/2021 Q5.





2021 October/November · 9231/11 & /13 · Question 6 · 7 marks
\(C:r=2\cos\theta(1+\sin\theta)\) for \(0\leqslant\theta\leqslant\pi/2\).
(a) Find the point furthest from the pole. [5] (b) Sketch \(C\). [2]


Show answer and mark scheme

Differentiating gives
\[\frac{dr}{d\theta}=2\{\cos^2\theta-(1+\sin\theta)\sin\theta\}=0.\]
Thus \(1-sin\theta-2\sin^2\theta=0\), so \(\sin\theta=1/2\) in the interval. Hence
\[\boxed{(r,\theta)=\left(\frac{3\sqrt3}{2},\frac\pi6\right)}.\]
The curve begins at \((2,0)\), reaches this maximum, then is tangent to \(\theta=\pi/2\) at the pole.



2021 O/N 11–13

The maximum radius occurs at θ = π/6.   2021 O/N 11–13 initial lineyOmaximum


The maximum radius occurs at θ = π/6.




Sources: 9231/11/O/N/2021 Q6; 9231/13/O/N/2021 Q6.





2021 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 5 · 12 marks
\(C:r=3+2\sin\theta\) for \(-\pi<\theta\leqslant\pi\), and \(l:r\sin\theta=2\).
(a) Complete the sketch. [1] (b) Add \(l\) and find both intersections. [5] (c) Find exactly the area enclosed by \(C\) and \(l\) that contains the pole. [6]


Show answer and mark scheme

\(l\) is \(y=2\). At an intersection,
\[2=(3+2\sin\theta)\sin\theta,\]
giving \(\sin\theta=1/2\). Therefore the intersections are
\[\boxed{(4,\pi/6)},\;\boxed{(4,5\pi/6)}.\]
Using symmetry, the curved part with two radii has area
\[2\cdot\frac12\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/6}(3+2\sin\theta)^2d\theta
=\frac{22\pi}{3}-\frac{13\sqrt3}{2}.\]
Adding the two congruent triangles gives \(4\cos(\pi/6)\times2=4\sqrt3\). Hence
\[\boxed{A=\frac{22\pi}{3}-\frac{5\sqrt3}{2}}.\]



2021 O/N 12: curve and y = 2

The horizontal line y = 2 cuts the symmetric closed curve at two points.   2021 O/N 12: curve and y = 2 initial lineyOC(4, π/6)(4, 5π/6)


The horizontal line y = 2 cuts the symmetric closed curve at two points.




Source: 9231/12/O/N/2021 Q5.




2022



2022 May/June · 9231/11 & /12 · Question 6 · 13 marks
\(C:r^2=\tan^{-1}(\theta/2)\) for \(0\leqslant\theta\leqslant2\).
(a) Sketch \(C\) and state exactly its greatest radius. [3]
(b) Find exactly the area bounded by \(C\) and \(\theta=2\). [5]
For \(0\leqslant\theta\leqslant\pi/2\), (c) show that the point furthest from \(\theta=\pi/2\) satisfies
\[
(\theta^2+4)\tan^{-1}(\theta/2)\sin\theta-\cos\theta=0,
\]
and verify a root in \((0.6,0.7)\). [5]


Show answer and mark scheme

\(r\) increases throughout the interval, so
\[r_{\max}=\sqrt{\tan^{-1}1}=\boxed{\frac{\sqrt\pi}{2}}.\]
For the area, integration by parts gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
A&=\frac12\int_0^2\tan^{-1}(\theta/2)d\theta\\
&=\frac12\left[\theta\tan^{-1}(\theta/2)-\ln(\theta^2+4)\right]_0^2\\
&=\boxed{\frac\pi4-\frac12\ln2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For part (c), the perpendicular distance is
\[x=r\cos\theta=\{  an^{-1}(\theta/2)\}^{1/2}\cos\theta.\]
Setting \(dx/d\theta=0\) and clearing the positive factors gives the required equation. Its left side is
\[-0.108\text{ at }\theta=0.6,\; 0.209\text{ at }\theta=0.7,\]
so the root is verified.



2022 M/J 11–12

The radius increases to √π/2.   2022 M/J 11–12 initial lineyOθ = 2


The radius increases to √π/2.




Sources: 9231/11/M/J/2022 Q6; 9231/12/M/J/2022 Q6.





2022 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 6 · 13 marks
\(C\) has Cartesian equation \(x^2+xy+y^2=a\), where \(a>0\).
(a) Show that
\[r^2=\frac{2a}{2+\sin2\theta}.\]
[3] (b) Sketch the part for \(0\leqslant\theta\leqslant\pi/4\). [2]
(c) Find exactly the area enclosed by this part, the initial line and \(\theta=\pi/4\). [8]


Show answer and mark scheme

Substituting \(x=r\cos\theta\) and \(y=r\sin\theta\) gives
\[r^2(1+\sin\theta\cos\theta)=a,\]
hence
\[\boxed{r^2=\frac{2a}{2+\sin2\theta}}.\]
The radius decreases smoothly from \(\sqrt a\) at \(\theta=0\) to \(\sqrt{2a/3}\) at \(\theta=\pi/4\).
Using \(t=\tan\theta\) and \(dt=(1+t^2)d\theta\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
A&=\frac12\int_0^{\pi/4}r^2d\theta
=\frac a2\int_0^1\frac{dt}{t^2+t+1}\\
&=\frac a2\int_0^1\frac{dt}{(t+1/2)^2+3/4}\\
&=\frac a{\sqrt3}\left[\tan^{-1}\frac{2t+1}{\sqrt3}\right]_0^1\\
&=\boxed{\frac{\pi a}{6\sqrt3}}.
\end{aligned}
\]



2022 M/J 13

Scaled with a = 1; the radius decreases on 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/4.   2022 M/J 13 initial lineyOθ = π/4


Scaled with a = 1; the radius decreases on 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/4.




Source: 9231/13/M/J/2022 Q6.




2023



2023 October/November · 9231/11 & /13 · Question 6 · 15 marks
(a) Show that \((x-1/2)^2+y^2=1/4\) has polar equation \(r=\cos\theta\). [3]
\(C_1:r=\cos\theta\) and \(C_2:r=\sin2\theta\) for \(0\leqslant\theta\leqslant\pi/2\) meet at the pole and \(P\).
(b) Find \(P\). [3] (c) Sketch both curves and mark \(P\). [3] (d) Find exactly the enclosed area containing \(OP\). [6]


Show answer and mark scheme

Expanding the Cartesian equation gives \(x^2-x+y^2=0\), hence
\[r^2-r\cos\theta=0\Longrightarrow\boxed{r=\cos\theta}.\]
At the non-pole intersection,
\[\sin2\theta=\cos\theta\Longrightarrow 2\sin\theta=1,\]
so
\[\boxed{P\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2},\frac\pi6\right)}.\]
\(C_2\) bounds the region for \(0\leqslant\theta\leqslant\pi/6\), and \(C_1\) for \(\pi/6\leqslant\theta\leqslant\pi/2\). Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
A&=\frac12\int_0^{\pi/6}\sin^22\theta\,d\theta
+\frac12\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/2}\cos^2\theta\,d\theta\\
&=\boxed{\frac\pi8-\frac{3\sqrt3}{32}}.
\end{aligned}
\]



2023 O/N 11–13: C₁ and C₂

The required region is bounded by different curves on either side of P.   2023 O/N 11–13: C₁ and C₂ initial lineyOC₁C₂P


The required region is bounded by different curves on either side of P.




Sources: 9231/11/O/N/2023 Q6; 9231/13/O/N/2023 Q6.





2023 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 6 · 13 marks
\[C:r=e^{-\theta}-e^{-\pi/2},\;0\leqslant\theta\leqslant\pi/2.\]
(a) Sketch \(C\) and state exactly its greatest radius. [3] (b) Find exactly the area bounded by \(C\) and the initial line. [5]
(c) Show that the point furthest from the initial line satisfies
\[1-e^{\theta-\pi/2}-\tan\theta=0,\]
and verify a root in \((0.56,0.57)\). [5]


Show answer and mark scheme

\(r\) decreases from \(1-e^{-\pi/2}\) to \(0\), so the greatest radius is
\[\boxed{1-e^{-\pi/2}}.\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
A&=\frac12\int_0^{\pi/2}(e^{-\theta}-e^{-\pi/2})^2d\theta\\
&=\boxed{\frac14-e^{-\pi/2}+\frac{\pi+3}{4}e^{-\pi}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The distance from the initial line is
\[y=(e^{-\theta}-e^{-\pi/2})\sin\theta.\]
Setting \(dy/d\theta=0\) and dividing by \(e^{-\theta}\cos\theta\) gives the stated equation. Its values at \(0.56\) and \(0.57\) have opposite signs, so the root is verified.



2023 O/N 12

The radius decreases from 1 − e^(−π/2) to the pole.   2023 O/N 12 initial lineyO


The radius decreases from 1 − e^(−π/2) to the pole.




Source: 9231/12/O/N/2023 Q6.




2024



2024 May/June · 9231/11 & /12 · Question 7 · 15 marks
\(C:r^2=(\pi-\theta)\tan^{-1}(\pi-\theta)\) for \(0\leqslant\theta\leqslant\pi\).
(a) Sketch \(C\) and state the point furthest from the pole. [3]
(b) Find the area enclosed by \(C\) and the initial line. [7]
(c) Show that the point furthest from the initial line satisfies
\[2(\pi-\theta)\tan^{-1}(\pi-\theta)\cot\theta-
\frac{\pi-\theta}{1+(\pi-\theta)^2}-\tan^{-1}(\pi-\theta)=0,\]
and verify a root in \((1.2,1.3)\). [5]


Show answer and mark scheme

\(r\) decreases to the pole, so the furthest point is
\[\boxed{\left(\sqrt{\pi\tan^{-1}\pi},0\right)}.\]
With \(u=\pi-\theta\) and integration by parts,
\[
\begin{aligned}
A&=\frac12\int_0^\pi u\tan^{-1}u\,du\\
&=\frac14(\pi^2+1)\tan^{-1}\pi-\frac\pi4.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(\boxed{A=\frac14\{(\pi^2+1)\tan^{-1}\pi-\pi\}}\).
For part (c), use \(y=r\sin\theta\) and differentiate \(y^2=r^2\sin^2\theta\). Clearing non-zero factors yields the stated equation; its two endpoint values have opposite signs.



2024 M/J 11–12

A decreasing-radius arc from the initial line to the pole.   2024 M/J 11–12 initial lineyO


A decreasing-radius arc from the initial line to the pole.




Sources: 9231/11/M/J/2024 Q7; 9231/12/M/J/2024 Q7.





2024 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 7 · 10 marks
\(C:r^2=\sin2\theta\cos\theta\) for \(0\leqslant\theta\leqslant\pi\).
(a) Sketch \(C\) and state its symmetry line. [3] (b) Find a Cartesian equation. [3] (c) Find the total enclosed area. [4]


Show answer and mark scheme

Since \(r^2\geqslant0\), the two loops occur for \(0\leqslant\theta\leqslant\pi/2\) and meet at the pole. They are symmetric about \(\boxed{\theta=\pi/2}\).
\[r^2=2\sin\theta\cos^2\theta.\]
Multiplying by \(r^3\) gives \(r^5=2(r\sin\theta)(r\cos\theta)^2=2yx^2\), so
\[\boxed{(x^2+y^2)^5=4x^4y^2}.\]
For both loops,
\[A=\frac12\int_0^\pi\sin2\theta\cos\theta,d\theta
=\int_0^\pi\sin\theta\cos^2\theta,d\theta
=\boxed{\frac23}.\]



2024 M/J 13

Two loops symmetric about θ = π/2.   2024 M/J 13 initial lineyOθ = π/2


Two loops symmetric about θ = π/2.




Source: 9231/13/M/J/2024 Q7.





2024 October/November · 9231/11 & /13 · Question 5 · 13 marks
(a) Show that \((x^2+y^2)^2=6xy\) has polar equation \(r^2=3\sin2\theta\). [2]
For \(0\leqslant\theta\leqslant\pi/2\), (b) sketch \(C\) and state its maximum radius; [3] (c) find the enclosed area; [2] (d) find the maximum distance from the initial line. [6]


Show answer and mark scheme

Substitution gives \(r^4=6r^2\sin\theta\cos\theta\), hence \(\boxed{r^2=3\sin2\theta}\).
The loop is symmetric about \(\theta=\pi/4\) and its maximum radius is \(\boxed{\sqrt3}\). Its area is
\[\frac12\int_0^{\pi/2}3\sin2\theta,d\theta=\boxed{\frac32}.\]
For the distance \(y=r\sin\theta\), maximise
\[y^2=3\sin2\theta\sin^2\theta=6\sin^3\theta\cos\theta.\]
Differentiation gives \(3\cos^2\theta=\sin^2\theta\), so \(\theta=\pi/3\) and
\[\boxed{y_{\max}=\sqrt{\frac{9\sqrt3}{8}}}.\]



2024 O/N 11–13

A loop symmetric about θ = π/4 with maximum radius √3.   2024 O/N 11–13 initial lineyOθ = π/4


A loop symmetric about θ = π/4 with maximum radius √3.




Sources: 9231/11/O/N/2024 Q5; 9231/13/O/N/2024 Q5.





2024 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 7 · 16 marks
\(C_1:r=a(\cos\theta+\sin\theta)\) for \(-\pi/4\leqslant\theta\leqslant3\pi/4\).
(a) Find its Cartesian equation, centre and radius. [4] (b) Sketch it and state its greatest radius. [3]
\(C_2:r=a\theta\) meets \(C_1\) at the pole and \((a\phi,\phi)\).
(c) Verify \(1.25<\phi<1.26\). [2]
(d) Show that the smaller enclosed area is
\[\frac{a^2}{2}\left(\frac{\phi^3}{3}+\frac{3\pi}{4}-\phi+\frac12\cos2\phi\right),\]
and deduce the larger area. [7]


Show answer and mark scheme

\(r^2=a(x+y)\) gives
\[\boxed{(x-a/2)^2+(y-a/2)^2=a^2/2}.\]
Thus the centre is \((a/2,a/2)\), the radius is \(a/\sqrt2\), and the greatest polar radius is \(\boxed{a\sqrt2}\).
At the non-pole intersection,
\[\cos\phi+\sin\phi-\phi=0.\]
The left side is positive at \(1.25\) and negative at \(1.26\), verifying the interval.
The smaller area is
\[\frac{a^2}{2}\left\{\int_0^\phi\theta^2d\theta+
\int_\phi^{3\pi/4}(\cos\theta+\sin\theta)^2d\theta\right\},\]
which gives the stated expression. Since the circle has area \(\pi a^2/2\), the larger area is
\[\boxed{\frac{a^2}{2}\left(\frac\pi4+\phi-\frac{\phi^3}{3}-\frac12\cos2\phi\right)}.\]



2024 O/N 12: circle and spiral

Scaled with a = 1; the circle and spiral meet at φ ≈ 1.259.   2024 O/N 12: circle and spiral initial lineyOC₁C₂P


Scaled with a = 1; the circle and spiral meet at φ ≈ 1.259.




Source: 9231/12/O/N/2024 Q7.




2025



2025 May/June · 9231/11 & /12 · Question 5 · 13 marks
\(C:r=\theta e^{\theta/8}\) for \(0\leqslant\theta\leqslant2\pi\).
(a) Sketch \(C\). [2] (b) Find the area bounded by \(C\) and the initial line in the form \((p\pi^2+q\pi+r)e^{\pi/2}+s\). [6]
(c) Show that the point furthest from the initial line satisfies
\[\theta\cos\theta+(\theta/8+1)\sin\theta=0,\]
and verify a root in \((5,5.05)\). [5]


Show answer and mark scheme

The curve is an anticlockwise outward spiral from the pole. For the area,
\[
A=\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}\theta^2e^{\theta/4}d\theta
=\boxed{(8\pi^2-32\pi+64)e^{\pi/2}-64}.
\]
Thus \((p,q,r,s)=(8,-32,64,-64)\). Differentiating
\[y=\theta e^{\theta/8}\sin\theta\]
gives the stated stationary equation. Substitution at \(5\) and \(5.05\) gives opposite signs.



2025 M/J 11–12

An outward anticlockwise spiral from θ = 0 to 2π.   2025 M/J 11–12 initial lineyO


An outward anticlockwise spiral from θ = 0 to 2π.




Sources: 9231/11/M/J/2025 Q5; 9231/12/M/J/2025 Q5.





2025 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 7 · 10 marks
\(C:r^2=e^{\sin\theta}\cos\theta\) for \(-\pi/2\leqslant\theta\leqslant\pi/2\).
(a) Find to \(3\) decimal places the point furthest from the pole. [5]
(b) Find to \(3\) decimal places the point furthest from the half-line \(\theta=\pi/2\). [5]


Show answer and mark scheme

For maximum \(r\), differentiate \(r^2\):
\[e^{\sin\theta}(\cos^2\theta-\sin\theta)=0.\]
Thus \(\sin\theta=(\sqrt5-1)/2\), giving
\[\boxed{(r,\theta)=(1.208,0.666)}.\]
Distance from \(\theta=\pi/2\) is \(x=r\cos\theta\). Maximising
\[x^2=e^{\sin\theta}\cos^3\theta\]
gives \(\cos^2\theta=3\sin\theta\), hence \(\sin\theta=(\sqrt{13}-3)/2\). Therefore
\[\boxed{(r,\theta)=(1.136,0.308)}.\]



2025 M/J 13

The two marked extrema are found by maximising r and r cos θ.   2025 M/J 13 initial lineyOmax rmax x


The two marked extrema are found by maximising r and r cos θ.




Source: 9231/13/M/J/2025 Q7.





2025 May/June · 9231/14 · Question 6 · 13 marks
\(C:r=a\tan(\theta/8)\) for \(a>0\) and \(0\leqslant\theta\leqslant2\pi\).
(a) Sketch \(C\) and state its greatest radius. [3] (b) Find its enclosed area. [4]
(c) Show that the point furthest from the initial line satisfies \(4\sin(\theta/4)\cos\theta+\sin\theta=0\), and verify a root in \((4.95,5)\). [6]


Show answer and mark scheme

\(r\) increases from \(0\) to \(a\), so \(\boxed{r_{\max}=a}\).
\[A=\frac{a^2}{2}\int_0^{2\pi}\tan^2(\theta/8)d\theta
=\boxed{a^2(4-\pi)}.\]
Differentiating \(y=a\tan(\theta/8)\sin\theta\) and simplifying with double-angle identities gives the stated equation; its signs at \(4.95\) and \(5\) differ.



2025 M/J 14

Scaled with a = 1; the spiral reaches r = a at θ = 2π.   2025 M/J 14 initial lineyO


Scaled with a = 1; the spiral reaches r = a at θ = 2π.




Source: 9231/14/M/J/2025 Q6.





2025 October/November · 9231/11 & /13 · Question 6 · 15 marks
\(C:r=\sin3\theta\) for \(0\leqslant\theta\leqslant\pi/3\).
(a) Sketch \(C\) and state its symmetry line. [3] (b) Find the enclosed area exactly. [4] (c) Find the maximum distance from the initial line. [5] (d) Find a Cartesian equation. [3]


Show answer and mark scheme

The single first-quadrant loop is symmetric about \(\boxed{\theta=\pi/6}\).
\[A=\frac12\int_0^{\pi/3}\sin^23\theta,d\theta=\boxed{\frac\pi{12}}.\]
Using \(\sin3\theta=3\sin\theta-4\sin^3\theta\),
\[y=r\sin\theta=3\sin^2\theta-4\sin^4\theta.\]
Stationarity gives \(\sin^2\theta=3/8\), and hence \(\boxed{y_{\max}=9/16}\).
Multiplying the polar equation by suitable powers of \(r\) gives
\[\boxed{(x^2+y^2)^2=y^2(3x^2-y^2)}.\]



2025 O/N 11–13

A single loop symmetric about θ = π/6.   2025 O/N 11–13 initial lineyOθ = π/6


A single loop symmetric about θ = π/6.




Sources: 9231/11/O/N/2025 Q6; 9231/13/O/N/2025 Q6.





2025 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 5 · 10 marks
\(C:r^2=\tan2\theta\) for \(0\leqslant\theta\leqslant\pi/8\).
(a) Sketch \(C\) and state its greatest radius. [2] (b) Find exactly the area bounded by \(C\) and \(\theta=\pi/8\). [4]
(c) Show that \(C\) has Cartesian equation \(x^4-2xy-y^4=0\), with the stated first-quadrant restrictions. [4]


Show answer and mark scheme

\(r\) increases from \(0\) to \(\boxed{1}\).
\[A=\frac12\int_0^{\pi/8}\tan2\theta,d\theta
=-\frac14[\ln(\cos2\theta)]_0^{\pi/8}
=\boxed{\frac18\ln2}.\]
Since
\[r^2=\frac{2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta},\]
cross-multiplication and substitution give
\[r^2(x^2-y^2)=2xy\Longrightarrow\boxed{x^4-2xy-y^4=0}.\]



2025 O/N 12

The radius increases from zero to one.   2025 O/N 12 initial lineyOθ = π/8


The radius increases from zero to one.




Source: 9231/12/O/N/2025 Q5.





2025 October/November · 9231/14 · Question 6 · 12 marks
\(C:r=\cos(\theta/2)\) for \(0\leqslant\theta\leqslant\pi\).
(a) Sketch \(C\). [2] (b) Find exactly the area enclosed by \(C\) and the initial line. [4] (c) Find the maximum distance from the initial line in the form \(p\sqrt q\). [6]


Show answer and mark scheme

The curve is a single arc from \((1,0)\) to the pole, lying in the first and second quadrants.
\[A=\frac12\int_0^\pi\cos^2(\theta/2)d\theta
=\frac14\int_0^\pi(1+\cos\theta)d\theta
=\boxed{\frac\pi4}.\]
For \(y=\cos(\theta/2)\sin\theta\), differentiation gives
\[\cos(\theta/2)\cos\theta-\frac12\sin\theta\sin(\theta/2)=0.\]
Using the given identities leads to \(\cos^2(\theta/2)=2/3\). Therefore
\[\boxed{y_{\max}=\frac{4\sqrt3}{9}}.\]



2025 O/N 14

A single arc from (1, 0) to the pole through the upper half-plane.   2025 O/N 14 initial lineyO


A single arc from (1, 0) to the pole through the upper half-plane.




Source: 9231/14/O/N/2025 Q6.

title: 1.5 Polar coordinates
text:
5. 完成本节的判断标准

坐标转换时能够正确判断角所在象限；
极坐标图能标出 pole、initial line、关键角、对称轴和 \(r\) 的极值；
遇到 \(r<0\) 时能按本课程约定截取正确区间；
求最远距离时能写出正确的 Cartesian 距离函数并检查端点；
面积题能从图形确定积分上下限，并完整写出代入、积分和精确值。

title: 1.3 Summation of series
text:
重要本节考纲要求



考生需要能够：

使用 \(\sum r\)、\(\sum r^2\)、\(\sum r^3\) 的标准结果求相关级数；
使用 method of differences 求有限级数之和，必要时先作部分分式分解；
直接考察前 \(n\) 项和，判断级数是否收敛，并在收敛时求无穷和。

title: 1.3 Summation of series
text:
学习路线


能从通项写出前几项，并从具体级数识别通项和求和上下限
能正确拆分求和符号并使用三个标准公式
能通过错位相减处理等比型有限和
能将有理式裂项，使中间项成对消去
能保留所有未消去的首项和尾项
能从 \(S_n\) 在 \(n\to\infty\) 时的极限判断收敛并求无穷和

title: 1.3 Summation of series
text:
1. 教材知识点

1.1 Sequences, series and sigma notation
数列是按顺序排列的数；级数是数列各项的和。若通项为 \(u_r\)，前 \(n\) 项和写作
\[
S_n=\sum_{r=1}^{n}u_r.
\]
上下限决定所包含的项。若求和式中没有 \(r\)，仍需按上下限重复相加，例如
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}c=nc.
\]
若已知前 \(n\) 项和，则
\[
u_1=S_1,\qquad u_r=S_r-S_{r-1}\quad(r\ge2).
\]


1.2 Standard results
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}r=\frac12n(n+1),
\]
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}r^2=\frac16n(n+1)(2n+1),
\]
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}r^3=\frac14n^2(n+1)^2.
\]
使用时先展开通项，再利用求和的线性性质。不要把 \(\sum r^2\) 误写成 \(\left(\sum r\right)^2\)。


1.3 Changing limits
对于连续的一段整数，可用“大和减小和”：
\[
\sum_{r=a}^{b}u_r
=\sum_{r=1}^{b}u_r-\sum_{r=1}^{a-1}u_r.
\]
同理，若 \(S_n=\sum_{r=1}^{n}u_r\)，则
\[
\sum_{r=n+1}^{2n}u_r=S_{2n}-S_n.
\]


1.4 Method of differences
核心是把通项写成相邻项之差：
\[
u_r=f(r)-f(r+1).
\]
于是
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}u_r
=[f(1)-f(2)]+[f(2)-f(3)]+\cdots+[f(n)-f(n+1)],
\]
中间项全部消去，只剩
\[
\boxed{S_n=f(1)-f(n+1)}.
\]
若裂项跨度大于 1，通常会留下多于一个首项和尾项，必须将前几项与最后几项完整写出。


1.5 Sum to infinity
先求有限前 \(n\) 项和 \(S_n\)，再直接考察
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}S_n.
\]
若极限存在且有限，则级数收敛，且该极限就是无穷和。若 \(u_n\not\to0\)，级数一定不收敛；但 \(u_n\to0\) 本身不能保证收敛。

title: 1.3 Summation of series
text:
2. Textbook Examples

Example 2.1 · Pages 43–44
For the series
\[
2+5+8+\cdots+500,
\]
(i) find a formula for the \(r\)th term \(u_r\); (ii) find the number of terms; (iii) find the sum by reversing and adding; (iv) confirm the answer using sigma notation.


Show solution

The sequence has common difference \(3\), so
\[
u_r=3r-1.
\]
Since \(3r-1=500\), there are \(167\) terms. Reversing and adding gives
\[
2S=167(2+500),
\]
so
\[
\boxed{S=41917}.
\]
Also
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{167}(3r-1)
=3\cdot\frac{167\cdot168}{2}-167
=41917.
\]

 Completed


Example 2.2 · Page 44
Calculate the sum of the integers from \(100\) to \(200\) inclusive.


Show solution

\[
\sum_{r=100}^{200}r
=\sum_{r=1}^{200}r-\sum_{r=1}^{99}r
=\frac{200\cdot201}{2}-\frac{99\cdot100}{2}.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{15150}.
\]

 Completed


Example 2.3 · Page 47
Given \(u_r=r^2+2r-1\):

write down the first three terms;
find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}u_r\);
check the result for \(n=3\).



Show solution

The first three terms are \(2,7,14\). Also
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{r=1}^{n}(r^2+2r-1)
&=\sum r^2+2\sum r-\sum1\\
&=\frac16n(n+1)(2n+1)+n(n+1)-n\\
&=\boxed{\frac16n(2n^2+9n+1)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(n=3\), the formula gives \(23\), and \(2+7+14=23\).

 Completed


Example 2.4 · Page 48
Write
\[
(1\times3)+(2\times4)+(3\times5)+\cdots+n(n+2)
\]
using sigma notation, and hence find its sum.


Show solution

\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}r(r+2)
=\sum_{r=1}^{n}(r^2+2r).
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\sum_{r=1}^{n}r(r+2)=\frac16n(n+1)(2n+7)}.
\]

 Completed


Example 2.5 · Page 50
Calculate
\[
5+10+20+40+\cdots+2560+5120.
\]


Show solution

Let the sum be \(S\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
S&=5+10+20+\cdots+2560+5120,\\
2S&=10+20+40+\cdots+5120+10240.
\end{aligned}
\]
Subtracting gives \(S=10240-5\), hence
\[
\boxed{S=10235}.
\]

 Completed


Example 2.6 · Pages 50–51
(i) Show that
\[
\frac1r-\frac1{r+1}=\frac1{r(r+1)}.
\]
(ii) Hence find
\[
\frac1{1\times2}+\frac1{2\times3}+\cdots+\frac1{30\times31}.
\]


Show solution

The identity follows by combining the two fractions. Therefore
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{30}\frac1{r(r+1)}
=\sum_{r=1}^{30}\left(\frac1r-\frac1{r+1}\right)
=1-\frac1{31}.
\]
Hence the sum is
\[
\boxed{\frac{30}{31}}.
\]

 Completed


Example 2.7 · Page 52
(i) Show that \((2r+1)^2-(2r-1)^2=8r\).
(ii) Hence find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}8r\).
(iii) Deduce the standard result for \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}r\).


Show solution

Expanding proves the identity. Summing gives
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}8r
=(3^2-1^2)+(5^2-3^2)+\cdots+[(2n+1)^2-(2n-1)^2].
\]
Thus
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}8r=(2n+1)^2-1=4n^2+4n,
\]
and hence
\[
\boxed{\sum_{r=1}^{n}r=\frac12n(n+1)}.
\]

 Completed


Example 2.8 · Pages 52–53
(i) Show that
\[
\frac2r-\frac3{r+1}+\frac1{r+2}
=\frac{r+4}{r(r+1)(r+2)}.
\]
(ii) Hence find
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac{r+4}{r(r+1)(r+2)}.
\]
(iii) Deduce the sum to infinity.


Show solution

After using the stated decomposition and writing the first and last terms, all middle terms cancel, leaving
\[
S_n=\frac32-\frac2{n+1}+\frac1{n+2}
=\frac{n(3n+7)}{2(n+1)(n+2)}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{S_\infty=\frac32}.
\]

 Completed

title: 1.3 Summation of series
section: 3. Cambridge examination questions in the textbook
text:
3. Cambridge examination questions in the textbook

Exercise 2B, Question 11
It is given that
\[
S_n=\sum_{r=1}^{n}u_r=2n^2+n.
\]
Write down \(S_1,S_2,S_3,S_4\). Express \(u_r\) in terms of \(r\), justifying your answer. Find
\[
\sum_{r=n+1}^{2n}u_r.
\]


Show solution

\[
S_1=3,\quad S_2=10,\quad S_3=21,\quad S_4=36.
\]
For \(r\ge2\),
\[
u_r=S_r-S_{r-1}=4r-1,
\]
and this also gives \(u_1=3\). Finally,
\[
\sum_{r=n+1}^{2n}u_r=S_{2n}-S_n
=\boxed{6n^2+n}.
\]

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231 Paper 11, Question 3, October/November 2013.



Exercise 2C, Question 11
Given that
\[
u_k=\frac1{2k-1}-\frac1{2k+1},
\]
express \(\sum_{k=13}^{n}u_k\) in terms of \(n\) and deduce \(\sum_{k=13}^{\infty}u_k\).


Show solution

\[
\sum_{k=13}^{n}u_k
=\left(\frac1{25}-\frac1{27}\right)+\cdots+
\left(\frac1{2n-1}-\frac1{2n+1}\right)
=\boxed{\frac1{25}-\frac1{2n+1}}.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{\sum_{k=13}^{\infty}u_k=\frac1{25}}.
\]

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231 Paper 11, Question 1, October/November 2014.



Exercise 2C, Question 12
For positive integers \(n\),
\[
a_n=\frac{n+5}{n^2-n+1}-\frac{n+6}{n^2+n+1},
\]
and \(S_N=\sum_{n=1}^{N}a_n\). Find \(S_{30}\) correct to 3 decimal places and the least \(N\) for which \(S_N>4.9\).


Show solution

Successive terms telescope because the second fraction in \(a_n\) is the first fraction in \(a_{n+1}\). Thus
\[
S_N=6-\frac{N+6}{N^2+N+1}.
\]
Therefore
\[
S_{30}=6-\frac{36}{931}=\boxed{5.961}\quad\text{(3 d.p.)}.
\]
Checking successive values gives \(S_2<4.9\) and \(S_3>4.9\), so
\[
\boxed{N=3}.
\]

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231 Paper 11, Question 4, October/November 2015.



Exercise 2C, Question 13
Let \(f(r)=r(r+1)(r+2)\).

Show that \(f(r)-f(r-1)=3r(r+1)\).
Hence show that \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}r(r+1)=\frac13n(n+1)(n+2)\).
Using the standard result for \(\sum r\), deduce the standard result for \(\sum r^2\).
Find the sum

\[
1^2+2(2^2)+3^2+2(4^2)+\cdots+2(n-1)^2+n^2,
\]
where \(n\) is odd.


Show solution

Summing \(f(r)-f(r-1)=3r(r+1)\) gives
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}r(r+1)=\frac13n(n+1)(n+2).
\]
Since \(r(r+1)=r^2+r\),
\[
\sum r^2=\frac13n(n+1)(n+2)-\frac12n(n+1)
=\boxed{\frac16n(n+1)(2n+1)}.
\]
For the final series, add one extra copy of every even square to the usual sum of squares. With \(m=(n-1)/2\),
\[
\boxed{\frac16n(n+1)(2n+1)+\frac23m(m+1)(2m+1)}.
\]

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231 Paper 11, Question 4, October/November 2012.

title: 1.3 Summation of series
text:
4. Past-paper question bank

2019



2019 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 2 · 5 marks
Let
\[
u_n=\frac{4\sin\left(n-\frac12\right)\sin\frac12}{\cos(2n-1)+\cos1}.
\]
(i) Show that \(u_n=\sec n-\sec(n-1)\). [2]
(ii) Use the method of differences to find \(\sum_{n=1}^{N}u_n\). [2]
(iii) Explain why \(u_1+u_2+u_3+\cdots\) does not converge. [1]


Show answer and mark scheme

(i) Using the sum-to-product identities,
\[
\cos(2n-1)+\cos1=2\cos n\cos(n-1),
\]
and
\[
2\sin\left(n-\frac12\right)\sin\frac12
=\cos(n-1)-\cos n.
\]
Therefore
\[
u_n
=\frac{2\{\cos(n-1)-\cos n\}}{2\cos n\cos(n-1)}
=\boxed{\sec n-\sec(n-1)}.
\]
(ii) Writing the first few and final terms,
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{N}u_n
=(\sec1-1)+(\sec2-\sec1)+\cdots+(\sec N-\sec(N-1))
=\boxed{\sec N-1}.
\]
(iii) The sequence \(\sec N\) does not approach a finite limit as \(N\to\infty\); in particular, \(\cos N\) oscillates and can be arbitrarily close to \(0\). Hence the sequence of partial sums \(\sec N-1\) has no limit, so the infinite series diverges.

 Completed

Sources: Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2019, Q2; 9231/12/M/J/2019, Q2.





2019 October/November · 9231/11, 9231/12 & 9231/13 · Question 5 · 9 marks
Let
\[
S_N=\sum_{r=1}^{N}(5r+1)(5r+6),
\qquad
T_N=\sum_{r=1}^{N}\frac1{(5r+1)(5r+6)}.
\]
(i) Use standard results to show that
\[
S_N=\frac13N(25N^2+90N+83).
\]
[3]
(ii) Use the method of differences to express \(T_N\) in terms of \(N\). [4]
(iii) Find \(\lim_{N\to\infty}\dfrac{S_NT_N}{N^3}\). [2]


Show answer and mark scheme

(i) Expanding the summand,
\[
S_N=\sum_{r=1}^{N}(25r^2+35r+6)
=25\sum_{r=1}^{N}r^2+35\sum_{r=1}^{N}r+6N.
\]
Substituting the standard results,
\[
S_N
=\frac{25}{6}N(N+1)(2N+1)
+\frac{35}{2}N(N+1)+6N
\]
\[
=\boxed{\frac13N(25N^2+90N+83)}.
\]
(ii) Partial fractions give
\[
\frac1{(5r+1)(5r+6)}
=\frac15\left(\frac1{5r+1}-\frac1{5r+6}\right),
\]
Hence
\[
T_N=\frac15\left[
\left(\frac16-\frac1{11}\right)
+\left(\frac1{11}-\frac1{16}\right)
+\cdots
+\left(\frac1{5N+1}-\frac1{5N+6}\right)
\right].
\]
All intermediate terms cancel, so
\[
\boxed{T_N=\frac1{30}-\frac1{5(5N+6)}}.
\]
(iii) From the leading terms,
\[
\frac{S_N}{N^3}\longrightarrow\frac{25}{3},
\qquad
T_N\longrightarrow\frac1{30}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{S_NT_N}{N^3}=\frac5{18}}.
\]

 Completed

Sources: Cambridge International 9231/11/O/N/2019, Q5; 9231/12/O/N/2019, Q5; 9231/13/O/N/2019, Q5.




2020



2020 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 4 · 10 marks
(a) By first expressing \(1/(r^2-1)\) in partial fractions, show that
\[
\sum_{r=2}^{n}\frac1{r^2-1}
=\frac34-\frac{2n+1}{2n(n+1)}.
\]
[5]
(b) Deduce \(\sum_{r=2}^{3}\frac1{r^2-1}\). [1]
(c) Find \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{r=n+1}^{2n}\frac1{r^2-1}\). [4]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) Since \(r^2-1=(r-1)(r+1)\),
\[
\frac1{r^2-1}
=\frac12\left(\frac1{r-1}-\frac1{r+1}\right).
\]
Therefore
\[
\sum_{r=2}^{n}\frac1{r^2-1}
=\frac12\left[
\left(1-\frac13\right)
+\left(\frac12-\frac14\right)
+\left(\frac13-\frac15\right)
+\cdots
+\left(\frac1{n-1}-\frac1{n+1}\right)
\right]
\]
\[
=\frac12\left(1+\frac12-\frac1n-\frac1{n+1}\right)
=\frac34-\frac{2n+1}{2n(n+1)},
\]
as required.
(b) Put \(n=3\) in part (a):
\[
\sum_{r=2}^{3}\frac1{r^2-1}=\boxed{\frac{11}{24}}.
\]
(c) Let \(F(n)=\sum_{r=2}^{n}1/(r^2-1)\). Then
\[
\sum_{r=n+1}^{2n}\frac1{r^2-1}=F(2n)-F(n).
\]
Using part (a),
\[
F(2n)-F(n)
=\left(\frac34-\frac{4n+1}{4n(2n+1)}\right)
-\left(\frac34-\frac{2n+1}{2n(n+1)}\right).
\]
Both remaining fractions tend to \(0\), so
\[
\boxed{0}.
\]

 Completed

Sources: Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2020, Q4; 9231/12/M/J/2020, Q4.





2020 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 3 · 8 marks
Let
\[
S_n=2^2+6^2+10^2+\cdots+(4n-2)^2.
\]
(a) Use standard results to show that
\[
S_n=\frac43n(4n^2-1).
\]
[4]
(b) Express \(n/S_n\) in partial fractions and find \(\sum_{n=1}^{N}n/S_n\). [4]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a)
\[
S_n=\sum_{r=1}^{n}(4r-2)^2
=\sum_{r=1}^{n}(16r^2-16r+4).
\]
Hence
\[
S_n
=\frac{16}{6}n(n+1)(2n+1)-8n(n+1)+4n
\]
\[
=\frac43n(4n^2-1),
\]
as required.
(b) Therefore
\[
\frac{n}{S_n}=\frac3{4(2n-1)(2n+1)}
=\frac38\left(\frac1{2n-1}-\frac1{2n+1}\right).
\]
Writing the terms explicitly,
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{n}{S_n}
=\frac38\left[
\left(1-\frac13\right)
+\left(\frac13-\frac15\right)
+\cdots
+\left(\frac1{2N-1}-\frac1{2N+1}\right)
\right].
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{n}{S_n}=\frac38\left(1-\frac1{2N+1}\right)
=\frac{3N}{4(2N+1)}}.
\]

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231/13/M/J/2020, Q3.





2020 October/November · 9231/13 · Question 2 · 7 marks
(a) Use standard results to find
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}(7r+1)(7r+8)
\]
as a cubic polynomial in \(n\). [3]
(b) Use the method of differences to find
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac1{(7r+1)(7r+8)}.
\]
[4]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) Since
\[
(7r+1)(7r+8)=49r^2+63r+8,
\]
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}(7r+1)(7r+8)
=49\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}6
+63\frac{n(n+1)}2+8n
\]
\[
=\boxed{\frac n3(49n^2+168n+143)}.
\]
(b) Partial fractions give
\[
\frac1{(7r+1)(7r+8)}
=\frac17\left(\frac1{7r+1}-\frac1{7r+8}\right),
\]
Hence
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac1{(7r+1)(7r+8)}
=\frac17\left[
\left(\frac18-\frac1{15}\right)
+\left(\frac1{15}-\frac1{22}\right)
+\cdots
+\left(\frac1{7n+1}-\frac1{7n+8}\right)
\right]
\]
\[
=\frac17\left(\frac18-\frac1{7n+8}\right),
\]
so
\[
\boxed{\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac1{(7r+1)(7r+8)}
=\frac n{8(7n+8)}}.
\]

 Completed

Sources: Cambridge International 9231/11/O/N/2020, Q2; 9231/13/O/N/2020, Q2.





2020 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 3 · 7 marks
(a) By simplifying
\[
(x^n-\sqrt{x^{2n}+1})(x^n+\sqrt{x^{2n}+1}),
\]
show that
\[
\frac1{x^n-\sqrt{x^{2n}+1}}=-x^n-\sqrt{x^{2n}+1}.
\]
[1]
Let
\[
u_n=x^{n+1}+\sqrt{x^{2n+2}+1}
+\frac1{x^n-\sqrt{x^{2n}+1}}.
\]
(b) Use the method of differences to find \(\sum_{n=1}^{N}u_n\). [3]
(c) Deduce the values of \(x\) for which the infinite series converges and give its sum. [3]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) The product is a difference of two squares:
\[
(x^n-\sqrt{x^{2n}+1})(x^n+\sqrt{x^{2n}+1})
=x^{2n}-(x^{2n}+1)=-1.
\]
Dividing by \(x^n-\sqrt{x^{2n}+1}\) gives the stated identity.
(b) Using part (a),
\[
u_n=\left(x^{n+1}+\sqrt{x^{2n+2}+1}\right)
-\left(x^n+\sqrt{x^{2n}+1}\right).
\]
Thus the sum is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=1}^{N}u_n
={}&\left(x^2+\sqrt{x^4+1}-x-\sqrt{x^2+1}\right)\\
&+\left(x^3+\sqrt{x^6+1}-x^2-\sqrt{x^4+1}\right)+\cdots\\
&+\left(x^{N+1}+\sqrt{x^{2N+2}+1}-x^N-\sqrt{x^{2N}+1}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
All intermediate terms cancel, giving
\[
\boxed{\sum_{n=1}^{N}u_n
=x^{N+1}+\sqrt{x^{2N+2}+1}-x-\sqrt{x^2+1}}.
\]
(c) A finite limit requires \(x^{N+1}\to0\), which occurs precisely when \(|x|<1\). Then
\[
\sqrt{x^{2N+2}+1}\longrightarrow1.
\]
Therefore the series converges for \(-1<x<1\), and its sum is
\[
\boxed{1-x-\sqrt{x^2+1}}.
\]

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231/12/O/N/2020, Q3.




2021



2021 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 2 · 9 marks
(a) Use standard results to find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}(1-r-r^2)\). [3]
(b) Show that
\[
\frac{1-r-r^2}{(r^2+2r+2)(r^2+1)}
=\frac{r+1}{(r+1)^2+1}-\frac r{r^2+1},
\]
and hence find the corresponding sum from \(r=1\) to \(n\). [5]
(c) Deduce the sum to infinity. [1]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a)
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}(1-r-r^2)
=n-\frac{n(n+1)}2-\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}6
\]
\[
=\boxed{-\frac13n(n^2+3n-1)}.
\]
(b) Combining the fractions on the right gives
\[
\frac{(r+1)(r^2+1)-r\{(r+1)^2+1\}}
{\{(r+1)^2+1\}(r^2+1)}
=\frac{1-r-r^2}{(r^2+2r+2)(r^2+1)},
\]
which proves the identity. Therefore
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left[
\frac{r+1}{(r+1)^2+1}-\frac r{r^2+1}
\right]
\]
\[
=\left(\frac25-\frac12\right)
+\left(\frac3{10}-\frac25\right)
+\cdots
+\left(\frac{n+1}{(n+1)^2+1}-\frac n{n^2+1}\right).
\]
The intermediate terms cancel, giving
\[

\qquad x>0.
\]

Show answer and mark scheme

(a) The defining difference telescopes:
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_n={}&\{x^{f(1)}-x^{f(2)}\}
+\{x^{f(2)}-x^{f(3)}\}+\cdots\\
&+\{x^{f(n)}-x^{f(n+1)}\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{S_n=x^{f(1)}-x^{f(n+1)}}.
\]
(b) For \(f(r)=\ln r\),
\[
x^{f(r)}=x^{\ln r}=r^{\ln x}.
\]
Since \(f(1)=0\),
\[
S_n=1-(n+1)^{\ln x}.
\]
If \(0<x<1\), then \(\ln x<0\) and \((n+1)^{\ln x}\to0\), so the sum is \(1\). If \(x=1\), every term is zero and the sum is \(0\). If \(x>1\), then \(\ln x>0\) and the partial sums have no finite limit. Thus the series converges for \(0<x\le1\), with the two sums stated above.

\[
x^{f(r)}=x^{2\log_x r}=r^2,
\]

\[
S_n=1-(n+1)^2=-n(n+2).
\]

\[
\sum_{n=1}^{N}S_n
=-\sum_{n=1}^{N}(n^2+2n)
=-\frac{N(N+1)(2N+1)}6-N(N+1)
\]
and hence
\[
\boxed{\sum_{n=1}^{N}S_n=-\frac16N(N+1)(2N+7)}.
\]

Show answer and mark scheme

(a) Expand the summand:
\[
(r+1)(r+2)(r+3)=r^3+6r^2+11r+6.
\]
Hence
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}(r+1)(r+2)(r+3)
=\left\{\frac{n(n+1)}2\right\}^2
+n(n+1)(2n+1)
+\frac{11}{2}n(n+1)+6n
\]
\[
=\frac14n(n^3+10n^2+35n+50).
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{b=10,\quad c=35,\quad d=50}.
\]
(b) Use
\[
\frac2{(r+1)(r+2)(r+3)}
=\frac1{(r+1)(r+2)}-\frac1{(r+2)(r+3)}.
\]
Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac2{(r+1)(r+2)(r+3)}
={}&\left(\frac1{2\cdot3}-\frac1{3\cdot4}\right)\\
&+\left(\frac1{3\cdot4}-\frac1{4\cdot5}\right)+\cdots\\
&+\left(\frac1{(n+1)(n+2)}-\frac1{(n+2)(n+3)}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
After cancellation,
\[
\boxed{\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac2{(r+1)(r+2)(r+3)}
=\frac16-\frac1{(n+2)(n+3)}}.
\]
(c) The final fraction tends to zero, so the sum to infinity is \(\boxed{\frac16}\).

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231/14/O/N/2025, Q3.

title: 1.3 Summation of series
text:
5. 完成本节的判断标准

能从具体各项准确写出通项及求和上下限；
能把多项式通项拆开并正确代入三个标准公式；
能从部分分式或恒等式识别消项结构；
能完整保留未消去的首项与尾项；
