title: 1.1 Roots of polynomial equations
text:
重要本节考纲要求



考生需要能够：

记忆并使用二次、三次及四次多项式方程的根与系数关系；
计算根的对称函数，或利用这些关系求方程中的未知系数；
通过代换建立新方程，新方程的根与原方程的根具有简单关系。

title: 1.1 Roots of polynomial equations
text:
学习路线


能从系数直接写出二次、三次和四次方程的根与系数关系
能把平方和、立方和等对称函数化为基本的根之和与根之积
能利用每个根都满足原方程来求较高次幂和
能用根与系数关系或代换法建立新方程
能根据给定的根之间的关系求未知系数并解方程

title: 1.1 Roots of polynomial equations
text:
1. 教材知识点

1.1 Quadratic equations
若 \(az^2+bz+c=0\) 的根为 \(\alpha,\beta\)，则
\[
\alpha+\beta=-\frac ba,
\qquad
\alpha\beta=\frac ca.
\]
二次方程中所有关于 \(\alpha,\beta\) 的对称函数，都可以用 \(\alpha+\beta\) 与 \(\alpha\beta\) 表示。例如
\[
\alpha^2+\beta^2=(\alpha+\beta)^2-2\alpha\beta.
\]


1.2 Cubic equations
若 \(az^3+bz^2+cz+d=0\) 的根为 \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\)，则
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum\alpha
&=\alpha+\beta+\gamma=-\frac ba,\\
\sum\alpha\beta
&=\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha=\frac ca,\\
\sum\alpha\beta\gamma
&=\alpha\beta\gamma=-\frac da.
\end{aligned}
\]
教材采用以下简写：
\[
\sum\alpha=\alpha+\beta+\gamma,
\qquad
\sum\alpha\beta=\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha.
\]


1.3 Common symmetric identities
对称函数的值不因根的排列次序改变。计算时通常先把所求式化为 \(\sum\alpha\)、\(\sum\alpha\beta\)、\(\alpha\beta\gamma\) 等基本对称函数。
对二次或三次方程的根，有
\[
\sum\alpha^2
=\left(\sum\alpha\right)^2-2\sum\alpha\beta.
\]
对三次方程的根，有
\[
\sum\alpha^3
=\left(\sum\alpha\right)^3
-3\left(\sum\alpha\right)\left(\sum\alpha\beta\right)
+3\alpha\beta\gamma,
\]
以及
\[
\sum\alpha^2\beta^2
=\left(\sum\alpha\beta\right)^2
-2\left(\sum\alpha\right)\alpha\beta\gamma,
\]
其中
\[
\sum\alpha^2\beta^2
=\alpha^2\beta^2+\beta^2\gamma^2+\gamma^2\alpha^2.
\]
展开或因式分解时，应让最终表达式只含原方程系数能够确定的基本对称函数。


1.4 Power sums
设三次方程的根为 \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\)，并定义
\[
S_n=\alpha^n+\beta^n+\gamma^n.
\]
若先把方程化为首一形式
\[
z^3+pz^2+qz+r=0,
\]
则
\[
S_0=3,
\qquad
S_1=-p,
\qquad
S_2=p^2-2q.
\]
因为每个根都满足原方程，将根的三个等式相加可得
\[
S_n+pS_{n-1}+qS_{n-2}+rS_{n-3}=0
\qquad(n\geqslant3).
\]
特别地，当 \(n=3\) 时，常数项会出现三次：
\[
S_3+pS_2+qS_1+3r=0.
\]
同理，若四次方程写成
\[
z^4+pz^3+qz^2+rz+s=0
\]
且 \(S_n\) 表示四个根的 \(n\) 次幂之和，则
\[
S_0=4
\]
并且
\[
S_n+pS_{n-1}+qS_{n-2}+rS_{n-3}+sS_{n-4}=0
\qquad(n\geqslant4).
\]
这种方法适合连续计算较高次幂和；开始递推前，应先由根与系数关系求出所需的较低次幂和。


1.5 Reciprocal roots and negative powers
若原方程的常数项不为零，则所有根都不为零，可以讨论倒数根。 对三次方程的根，
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac1\alpha+\frac1\beta+\frac1\gamma
&=\frac{\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha}{\alpha\beta\gamma},\\
\frac1{\alpha\beta}+\frac1{\beta\gamma}+\frac1{\gamma\alpha}
&=\frac{\alpha+\beta+\gamma}{\alpha\beta\gamma},\\
\frac1\alpha\frac1\beta\frac1\gamma
&=\frac1{\alpha\beta\gamma}.
\end{aligned}
\]
因此，若 \(az^3+bz^2+cz+d=0\) 的根为 \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\)，其中 \(d\ne0\)，则
\[
\sum\frac1\alpha=-\frac cd,
\qquad
\sum\frac1{\alpha\beta}=\frac bd,
\qquad
\frac1{\alpha\beta\gamma}=-\frac ad.
\]
求倒数根方程时，令 \(z=1/w\) 并乘以适当的 \(w\) 的幂。例如，
\[
az^3+bz^2+cz+d=0
\]
对应的倒数根方程为
\[
dw^3+cw^2+bw+a=0.
\]
也就是说，系数的次序反转。相同方法适用于二次及四次方程。
负次幂和可以看作倒数根的正次幂和。例如
\[
\sum\alpha^{-n}
=\left(\frac1\alpha\right)^n
+\left(\frac1\beta\right)^n
+\left(\frac1\gamma\right)^n,
\]
所以可以先建立倒数根方程，再使用上一节的幂和方法。


1.6 Forming new equations
教材使用两种方法建立新方程：

计算新根的和、两两乘积之和及乘积，再由根与系数关系写出方程；
令新变量与旧变量满足题目给出的根的变换，写出旧变量并代入原方程。

例如新根为 \(2\alpha+1,2\beta+1,2\gamma+1\) 时，令
\[
w=2z+1,
\qquad
z=\frac{w-1}{2}.
\]
新根为 \(\alpha^2,\beta^2,\gamma^2\) 时，可以令 \(w=z^2\)，再消去 \(z\)。


1.7 Quartic equations
若 \(az^4+bz^3+cz^2+dz+e=0\) 的根为 \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\)，则
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum\alpha
&=\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta=-\frac ba,\\
\sum\alpha\beta
&=\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\alpha\delta
+\beta\gamma+\beta\delta+\gamma\delta=\frac ca,\\
\sum\alpha\beta\gamma
&=\alpha\beta\gamma+\beta\gamma\delta
+\gamma\delta\alpha+\delta\alpha\beta=-\frac da,\\
\sum\alpha\beta\gamma\delta
&=\alpha\beta\gamma\delta=\frac ea.
\end{aligned}
\]






提示Sign pattern



从最高次项开始，根的基本对称函数对应的符号依次为
\[
-,\quad +,\quad -,\quad +.
\]

title: 1.1 Roots of polynomial equations
text:
2. Textbook examples and examination questions

Textbook Examples


Example 3.1 · Page 72
Find a quadratic equation with roots \(5\) and \(-3\).


Show solution

The sum of the roots is
\[
5+(-3)=2,
\]
and the product of the roots is
\[
5(-3)=-15.
\]
Taking the coefficient of \(z^2\) to be \(1\), a quadratic equation with the required roots is
\[
\boxed{z^2-2z-15=0}.
\]

 Completed


Example 3.2 · Page 73
The roots of the equation
\[
2z^2+3z+5=0
\]
are \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\).

Find the values of \(\alpha+\beta\) and \(\alpha\beta\).
Find the quadratic equation with roots \(2\alpha\) and \(2\beta\).



Show solution

From the original equation,
\[
\alpha+\beta=-\frac32,
\qquad
\alpha\beta=\frac52.
\]
For the new roots,
\[
2\alpha+2\beta=2(\alpha+\beta)=-3,
\]
and
\[
(2\alpha)(2\beta)=4\alpha\beta=10.
\]
Therefore the required equation is
\[
\boxed{z^2+3z+10=0}.
\]

 Completed


Example 3.3 · Pages 73–74
The roots of the equation
\[
3z^2-4z-1=0
\]
are \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). Find the quadratic equation with roots \(\alpha+1\) and \(\beta+1\).


Show solution

From the original equation,
\[
\alpha+\beta=\frac43,
\qquad
\alpha\beta=-\frac13.
\]
The sum of the new roots is
\[
(\alpha+1)+(\beta+1)=\alpha+\beta+2=\frac{10}{3},
\]
and their product is
\[
(\alpha+1)(\beta+1)
=\alpha\beta+(\alpha+\beta)+1
=2.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{3z^2-10z+6=0}.
\]

 Completed


Example 3.4 · Pages 74–75
The quadratic equation
\[
ax^2+bx+c=0,
\]
where \(a,b,c\) are constants, has roots \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). Prove that
\[
\alpha^2+\beta^2=\frac{b^2-2ac}{a^2}.
\]


Show solution

Since
\[
(\alpha+\beta)^2=\alpha^2+2\alpha\beta+\beta^2,
\]
we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
\alpha^2+\beta^2
&=(\alpha+\beta)^2-2\alpha\beta\\
&=\left(-\frac ba\right)^2-2\left(\frac ca\right)\\
&=\boxed{\frac{b^2-2ac}{a^2}}.
\end{aligned}
\]

 Completed


Example 3.5 · Page 78
The roots of the equation
\[
2z^3-9z^2-27z+54=0
\]
form a geometric progression, so they may be written as \(\dfrac ar,a,ar\). Solve the equation.


Show solution

Using the product of the roots,
\[
\frac ar\times a\times ar=-\frac{54}{2},
\]
so
\[
a^3=-27
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
a=-3.
\]
Using the sum of the roots,
\[
-\frac3r-3-3r=\frac92.
\]
Hence
\[
2r^2+5r+2=0,
\]
so
\[
(2r+1)(r+2)=0
\]
and therefore \(r=-2\) or \(r=-\dfrac12\). Either value gives the same three roots:
\[
\boxed{\frac32,-3,6}.
\]

 Completed


Example 3.6 · Pages 78–79
The roots of the cubic equation
\[
x^3-4x^2+x+6=0
\]
are \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\). Find the values of

\(\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2\);
\(\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3\).



Show solution

From the original equation,
\[
\sum\alpha=4,
\qquad
\sum\alpha\beta=1.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2
&=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^2
-2(\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha)\\
&=4^2-2(1)\\
&=\boxed{14}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since each root satisfies \(x^3-4x^2+x+6=0\),
\[
\alpha^3=4\alpha^2-\alpha-6,
\]
with corresponding equations for \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\). Adding them gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3
&=4(\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2)
-(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)-18\\
&=4(14)-4-18\\
&=\boxed{34}.
\end{aligned}
\]

 Completed


Example 3.7 · Pages 79–80
The roots of the cubic equation
\[
2z^3+5z^2-3z-2=0
\]
are \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\). Find the cubic equation with roots \(2\alpha+1,2\beta+1,2\gamma+1\).


Show solution 1: relations between roots and coefficients

For the original equation,
\[
\sum\alpha=-\frac52,
\qquad
\sum\alpha\beta=-\frac32,
\qquad
\alpha\beta\gamma=1.
\]
For the new roots, their sum is
\[
2(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)+3=-2.
\]
The sum of their products in pairs is
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(2\alpha+1)(2\beta+1)
+(2\beta+1)(2\gamma+1)
+(2\gamma+1)(2\alpha+1)\\
&=4(\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha)
+4(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)+3\\
&=4\left(-\frac32\right)+4\left(-\frac52\right)+3\\
&=-13.
\end{aligned}
\]
Their product is
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(2\alpha+1)(2\beta+1)(2\gamma+1)\\
&=8\alpha\beta\gamma
+4(\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha)
+2(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)+1\\
&=8+4\left(-\frac32\right)
+2\left(-\frac52\right)+1\\
&=-2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence the required equation is
\[
\boxed{z^3+2z^2-13z+2=0}.
\]



Show solution 2: substitution method

Let
\[
w=2z+1,
\qquad
z=\frac{w-1}{2}.
\]
Substituting into the original equation gives
\[
2\left(\frac{w-1}{2}\right)^3
+5\left(\frac{w-1}{2}\right)^2
-3\left(\frac{w-1}{2}\right)-2=0.
\]
Multiplying by \(4\) and simplifying,
\[
(w-1)^3+5(w-1)^2-6(w-1)-8=0,
\]
so
\[
\boxed{w^3+2w^2-13w+2=0}.
\]

 Completed


Example 3.8 · Pages 80–81
The roots of the cubic equation
\[
2z^3-5z^2+z+2=0
\]
are \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\). Find the cubic equation with roots \(\alpha^2,\beta^2,\gamma^2\).


Show solution

Let \(w=z^2\), so \(z=\sqrt w\). Substitution gives
\[
2w\sqrt w-5w+\sqrt w+2=0.
\]
Collecting the terms containing \(\sqrt w\),
\[
\sqrt w(2w+1)=5w-2.
\]
Squaring both sides,
\[
w(2w+1)^2=(5w-2)^2.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
4w^3+4w^2+w&=25w^2-20w+4,\\
4w^3-21w^2+21w-4&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore the required equation is
\[
\boxed{4w^3-21w^2+21w-4=0}.
\]

 Completed


Example 3.9 · Pages 84–85
The roots of the quartic equation
\[
4z^4+pz^3+qz^2-z+3=0
\]
are \(\alpha,-\alpha,\alpha+\lambda,\alpha-\lambda\), where \(\alpha\) and \(\lambda\) are real numbers.

Express \(p\) and \(q\) in terms of \(\alpha\) and \(\lambda\).
Show that \(\alpha=-\dfrac12\), and find the values of \(p\) and \(q\).
Give the roots of the quartic equation.



Show solution

The sum of the roots is
\[
\alpha-\alpha+(\alpha+\lambda)+(\alpha-\lambda)
=2\alpha=-\frac p4,
\]
so
\[
\boxed{p=-8\alpha}.
\]
The sum of the products of the roots in pairs simplifies to \(-\lambda^2\). Hence
\[
-\lambda^2=\frac q4
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\boxed{q=-4\lambda^2}.
\]
The sum of the products of the roots in threes is
\[
-2\alpha^3.
\]
Since this is equal to \(-\dfrac{-1}{4}=\dfrac14\),
\[
-2\alpha^3=\frac14.
\]
Thus
\[
\alpha^3=-\frac18
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\boxed{\alpha=-\frac12},
\]
and therefore
\[
\boxed{p=4}.
\]
Using the product of the four roots,
\[
-\alpha^2(\alpha^2-\lambda^2)=\frac34.
\]
Substituting \(\alpha=-\dfrac12\) gives
\[
-\frac14\left(\frac14-\lambda^2\right)=\frac34,
\]
so
\[
\lambda^2=\frac{13}{4}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\boxed{q=-13}.
\]
The roots are
\[
\boxed{
\frac12,
-\frac12,
-\frac12+\frac{\sqrt{13}}2,
-\frac12-\frac{\sqrt{13}}2
}.
\]

 Completed


Examination questions printed in the textbook exercises


Exercise 3B, Question 16
Source: 9231 Paper 11 Q5 October/November 2015
The cubic equation
\[
x^3+px^2+qx+r=0,
\]
where \(p,q,r\) are integers, has roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\) such that
\[
\alpha+\beta+\gamma=15,
\qquad
\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=83.
\]
Write down the value of \(p\) and find the value of \(q\).
Given that \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\) are all real and that \(\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma=36\), find \(\alpha\) and hence find the value of \(r\).


Show solution

Since \(\alpha+\beta+\gamma=-p\),
\[
\boxed{p=-15}.
\]
Also,
\[
\begin{aligned}
83
&=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^2
-2(\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha)\\
&=15^2-2q,
\end{aligned}
\]
so
\[
\boxed{q=71}.
\]
Now
\[
\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma
=\alpha(\beta+\gamma)
=\alpha(15-\alpha)=36.
\]
Thus
\[
\alpha^2-15\alpha+36=0,
\]
giving \(\alpha=3\) or \(\alpha=12\).
If \(\alpha=12\), then \(\beta+\gamma=3\) and \(\beta\gamma=35\), which does not give real values of \(\beta,\gamma\). Hence
\[
\boxed{\alpha=3}.
\]
Then \(\beta+\gamma=12\) and \(\beta\gamma=35\), so
\[
r=-\alpha\beta\gamma=-3(35)=\boxed{-105}.
\]

 Completed


Exercise 3B, Question 17
Source: 9231 Paper 11 Q2 October/November 2013
The cubic equation
\[
x^3-px-q=0,
\]
where \(p,q\) are constants, has roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\). Show that

\(\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=2p\);
\(\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3=3q\);
\[
6(\alpha^5+\beta^5+\gamma^5)
=5(\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3)
(\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2).
\]



Show solution

For the original equation,
\[
\alpha+\beta+\gamma=0,
\qquad
\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha=-p.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2
&=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^2
-2(\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha)\\
&=0-2(-p)\\
&=\boxed{2p}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Each root satisfies \(x^3=px+q\). Adding the three corresponding equations gives
\[
\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3
=p(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)+3q
=\boxed{3q}.
\]
Multiplying \(x^3=px+q\) by \(x^2\) gives \(x^5=px^3+qx^2\). Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
\alpha^5+\beta^5+\gamma^5
&=p(\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3)
+q(\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2)\\
&=p(3q)+q(2p)\\
&=5pq.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus both sides of the required identity are equal to \(30pq\).

 Completed


Exercise 3B, Question 18
Source: 9231 Paper 11 Q1 October/November 2011
The equation
\[
x^3+px+q=0
\]
has a repeated root. Prove that
\[
4p^3+27q^2=0.
\]


Show solution

Let the repeated root be \(\alpha\) and the third root be \(\beta\). Since the coefficient of \(x^2\) is zero,
\[
2\alpha+\beta=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\beta=-2\alpha.
\]
Using the sum of the products in pairs,
\[
p=\alpha^2+2\alpha\beta
=\alpha^2-4\alpha^2
=-3\alpha^2.
\]
Using the product of the roots,
\[
-q=\alpha^2\beta=-2\alpha^3,
\]
so \(q=2\alpha^3\). Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
4p^3+27q^2
&=4(-3\alpha^2)^3+27(2\alpha^3)^2\\
&=-108\alpha^6+108\alpha^6\\
&=\boxed{0}.
\end{aligned}
\]

 Completed


Exercise 3C, Question 7
Source: 9231 Paper 11 Q11 October/November 2014
The roots of the quartic equation
\[
x^4+4x^3+2x^2-4x+1=0
\]
are \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\). Find the values of

\(\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta\);
\(\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2+\delta^2\);
\(\dfrac1\alpha+\dfrac1\beta+\dfrac1\gamma+\dfrac1\delta\);
\[
\frac{\alpha}{\beta\gamma\delta}
+\frac{\beta}{\alpha\gamma\delta}
+\frac{\gamma}{\alpha\beta\delta}
+\frac{\delta}{\alpha\beta\gamma}.
\]

Using the substitution \(y=x+1\), find a quartic equation in \(y\). Solve this quartic equation and hence find the roots of
\[
x^4+4x^3+2x^2-4x+1=0.
\]


Show solution

From the coefficients,
\[
\sum\alpha=-4,
\qquad
\sum\alpha\beta=2,
\qquad
\sum\alpha\beta\gamma=4,
\qquad
\alpha\beta\gamma\delta=1.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta=-4},
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2+\delta^2
&=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta)^2-2\sum\alpha\beta\\
&=16-4\\
&=\boxed{12},
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\frac1\alpha+\frac1\beta+\frac1\gamma+\frac1\delta
=\frac{\sum\alpha\beta\gamma}{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}
=\boxed{4}.
\]
Also,
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{\alpha}{\beta\gamma\delta}
+\frac{\beta}{\alpha\gamma\delta}
+\frac{\gamma}{\alpha\beta\delta}
+\frac{\delta}{\alpha\beta\gamma}\\
&=\frac{\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2+\delta^2}
{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}\\
&=\boxed{12}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Let \(y=x+1\), so \(x=y-1\). Substitution gives
\[
y^4-4y^2+4=0,
\]
or
\[
(y^2-2)^2=0.
\]
Thus \(y=\pm\sqrt2\), each repeated, and the roots of the original equation are
\[
\boxed{-1+\sqrt2,\ -1+\sqrt2,\ -1-\sqrt2,\ -1-\sqrt2}.
\]

 Completed


Exercise 3C, Question 8
Source: 9231 Paper 11 Q11 October/November 2012
The roots of the equation
\[
x^4-3x^2+5x-2=0
\]
are \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\), and
\[
S_n=\alpha^n+\beta^n+\gamma^n+\delta^n.
\]
Show that
\[
S_{n+4}-3S_{n+2}+5S_{n+1}-2S_n=0.
\]
Find the values of

\(S_2\) and \(S_4\);
\(S_3\) and \(S_5\).

Hence find the value of
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\alpha^2(\beta^3+\gamma^3+\delta^3)
+\beta^2(\gamma^3+\delta^3+\alpha^3)\\
&\quad+\gamma^2(\delta^3+\alpha^3+\beta^3)
+\delta^2(\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3).
\end{aligned}
\]


Show solution

Each root satisfies
\[
x^4-3x^2+5x-2=0.
\]
Multiplying by \(x^n\) and then adding the four resulting equations gives
\[
\boxed{S_{n+4}-3S_{n+2}+5S_{n+1}-2S_n=0}.
\]
From the coefficients,
\[
S_1=0,
\qquad
\sum\alpha\beta=-3,
\]
so
\[
S_2=S_1^2-2\sum\alpha\beta=\boxed{6}.
\]
Taking \(n=0\) in the recurrence, with \(S_0=4\), gives
\[
S_4-3S_2+5S_1-2S_0=0,
\]
and hence
\[
S_4=\boxed{26}.
\]
Also, \(\sum\alpha\beta\gamma=-5\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_3
&=\left(\sum\alpha\right)^3
-3\left(\sum\alpha\right)\left(\sum\alpha\beta\right)
+3\sum\alpha\beta\gamma\\
&=0-0+3(-5)\\
&=\boxed{-15}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking \(n=1\) in the recurrence gives
\[
S_5-3S_3+5S_2-2S_1=0,
\]
so
\[
S_5=\boxed{-75}.
\]
The final expression is
\[
S_2S_3-S_5
=6(-15)-(-75)
=\boxed{-15}.
\]

 Completed

title: 1.1 Roots of polynomial equations
text:
3. Past-paper question bank

2019



2019 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 6 · 9 marks
Power sumsTransformed roots★★★☆☆
The equation
\[x^3-x+1=0\]
has roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\).
(i) Use the relation \(x=y^{1/3}\) to show that the equation
\[y^3+3y^2+2y+1=0\]
has roots \(\alpha^3,\beta^3,\gamma^3\). Hence write down the value of \(\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3\). [3]
Let \(S_n=\alpha^n+\beta^n+\gamma^n\).
(ii) Find the value of \(S_{-3}\). [2]
(iii) Show that \(S_6=5\) and find the value of \(S_9\). [4]


Show answer and mark scheme

(i) Put \(y=x^3\), so \(x=y^{1/3}\). Then
\[
y-y^{1/3}+1=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
y+1=y^{1/3}.
\]
Cubing both sides,
\[y=(y+1)^3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y^3+3y^2+2y+1=0. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]
The three roots are \(\alpha^3,\beta^3,\gamma^3\), so Vieta’s formula gives \(\boxed{S_3=-3}\). B1
(ii) For the roots \(\alpha^3,\beta^3,\gamma^3\), the sum of pairwise products is \(2\) and the product is \(-1\). Hence
\[S_{-3}=\frac{2}{-1}=-2. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]
(iii)
\[S_6=S_3^2-2(2)=(-3)^2-4=5. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]
Summing the transformed equation over its three roots gives
\[S_9+3S_6+2S_3+3=0,\]
so
\[S_9=-3(5)-2(-3)-3=-12. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]

 Completed

Sources: Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2019, Q6; 9231/12/M/J/2019, Q6.





2019 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 9 · 11 marks
Unknown coefficientsSymmetric sums★★★★☆
A cubic equation
\[x^3+bx^2+cx+d=0\]
has real roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\) such that
\[
\frac1\alpha+\frac1\beta+\frac1\gamma=-\frac5{12},
\qquad \alpha\beta\gamma=-12,
\qquad \alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3=90.
\]
(i) Find the values of \(c\) and \(d\). [3]
(ii) Express \(\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2\) in terms of \(b\). [2]
(iii) Show that \(b^3-15b+126=0\). [4]
(iv) Given that \(3+i\sqrt{12}\) is a root of \(y^3-15y+126=0\), deduce the value of \(b\). [2]


Show answer and mark scheme

(i) Since \(\alpha\beta\gamma=-d=-12\), \(d=12\). B1
Also
\[\frac{\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha}{\alpha\beta\gamma}=-\frac5{12},\]
so \(c=\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha=5\). M1 A1
(ii)
\[\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^2-2c=b^2-10. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]
(iii) Since \(S_2=b^2-10\) and every root satisfies \(x^3=-bx^2-5x-12\), summing over all three roots gives
\[90=-b(b^2-10)-5(-b)-36.\]
Hence
\[b^3-15b+126=0. \qquad \text{M1 M1 A1 A1}\]
(iv) The polynomial has real coefficients, so \(3-i\sqrt{12}\) is also a root. These two roots have sum \(6\). Since the coefficient of \(y^2\) is zero, the third root is \(-6\). Thus the required real value is \(\boxed{b=-6}\). M1 A1

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231/13/M/J/2019, Q9.





2019 October/November · 9231/11, 9231/12 & 9231/13 · Question 7 · 9 marks
Transformed rootsPower sums★★★★☆
The equation \(x^3+2x^2+x+7=0\) has roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\).
(i) Use the relation \(x^2=-7y\) to show that
\[49y^3+14y^2-27y+7=0\]
has roots
\[\frac{\alpha}{\beta\gamma},\qquad
\frac{\beta}{\gamma\alpha},\qquad
\frac{\gamma}{\alpha\beta}. \qquad \textbf{[4]}\]
(ii) Show that
\[\frac{\alpha^2}{\beta^2\gamma^2}+
\frac{\beta^2}{\gamma^2\alpha^2}+
\frac{\gamma^2}{\alpha^2\beta^2}=\frac{58}{49}. \qquad \textbf{[3]}\]
(iii) Find the exact value of
\[
\frac{\alpha^3}{\beta^3\gamma^3}+
\frac{\beta^3}{\gamma^3\alpha^3}+
\frac{\gamma^3}{\alpha^3\beta^3}. \qquad \textbf{[2]}
\]


Show answer and mark scheme

Since \(\alpha\beta\gamma=-7\),
\[\frac{\alpha}{\beta\gamma}=-\frac{\alpha^2}{7},\]
and similarly for the other two roots. With \(x^2=-7y\), the original equation becomes
\[
x(1-7y)+7(1-2y)=0,
\]
so \(x=7(2y-1)/(1-7y)\). Squaring and using \(x^2=-7y\) gives
\[
49(2y-1)^2=-7y(1-7y)^2,
\]
which simplifies to the stated cubic. M1 M1 A1 A1
For the transformed roots,
\[e_1=-\frac27,\qquad e_2=-\frac{27}{49},\qquad e_3=-\frac17.\]
Therefore
\[p_2=e_1^2-2e_2=\frac4{49}+\frac{54}{49}=\frac{58}{49}. \qquad \text{M1 A1 A1}\]
Also
\[p_3=e_1p_2-e_2p_1+3e_3=-\frac{317}{343}. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]

 Completed

Sources: Cambridge International 9231/11/O/N/2019, Q7; 9231/12/O/N/2019, Q7; 9231/13/O/N/2019, Q7.




2020



2020 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 2 · 8 marks
Squared rootsUnknown coefficient★★★☆☆
The cubic equation \(6x^3+px^2-3x-5=0\), where \(p\) is a constant, has roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\).
(a) Find a cubic equation whose roots are \(\alpha^2,\beta^2,\gamma^2\). [3]
(b) It is given that
\[\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=2(\alpha+\beta+\gamma).\]
(i) Find the value of \(p\). [3]
(ii) Find the value of \(\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3\). [2]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) Put \(y=x^2\). Rewriting the original equation gives \(x(6y-3)=5-py\). Squaring and using \(x^2=y\) gives
\[y(6y-3)^2=(5-py)^2,\]
hence
\[36y^3-(p^2+36)y^2+(10p+9)y-25=0. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}\]
(b)(i)
\[\alpha+\beta+\gamma=-\frac p6,\qquad
\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha=-\frac12.\]
Thus
\[\frac{p^2}{36}+1=-\frac p3,\]
so \((p+6)^2=0\) and \(p=-6\). M1 A1 A1
(b)(ii) With \(p=-6\),
\[e_1=1,\qquad e_2=-\frac12,\qquad e_3=\frac56,\]
and
\[\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3=e_1^3-3e_1e_2+3e_3=5. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]

 Completed

Sources: Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2020, Q2; 9231/12/M/J/2020, Q2.





2020 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 1 · 7 marks
Reciprocal rootsNegative powers★★★☆☆
The cubic equation \(7x^3+3x^2+5x+1=0\) has roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\).
(a) Find a cubic equation whose roots are \(\alpha^{-1},\beta^{-1},\gamma^{-1}\). [3]
(b) Find \(\alpha^{-2}+\beta^{-2}+\gamma^{-2}\). [2]
(c) Find \(\alpha^{-3}+\beta^{-3}+\gamma^{-3}\). [2]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) Put \(y=1/x\). Then
\[
\frac7{y^3}+\frac3{y^2}+\frac5y+1=0.
\]
Multiplying by \(y^3\) gives
\[y^3+5y^2+3y+7=0. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}\]
For the reciprocal roots, \(e_1=-5\), \(e_2=3\), \(e_3=-7\).
(b)
\[p_2=e_1^2-2e_2=25-6=19. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]
(c)
\[p_3=e_1p_2-e_2p_1+3e_3=-5(19)-3(-5)-21=-101. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231/13/M/J/2020, Q1.





2020 October/November · 9231/11 & 9231/13 · Question 3 · 11 marks
Cubed rootsSingular matrix★★★★☆
The cubic equation \(x^3+cx+1=0\), where \(c\) is a constant, has roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\).
(a) Find a cubic equation whose roots are \(\alpha^3,\beta^3,\gamma^3\). [3]
(b) Show that \(\alpha^6+\beta^6+\gamma^6=3-2c^3\). [3]
(c) Find the real value of \(c\) for which
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
1&\alpha^3&\beta^3\\
\alpha^3&1&\gamma^3\\
\beta^3&\gamma^3&1
\end{pmatrix}
\]
is singular. [5]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) Put \(y=x^3\). Since \(cx=-(y+1)\), cubing and using \(x^3=y\) gives \(c^3y=-(y+1)^3\), hence
\[y^3+3y^2+(c^3+3)y+1=0. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}\]
(b) For the new roots, \(e_1=-3\) and \(e_2=c^3+3\). Hence
\[\alpha^6+\beta^6+\gamma^6=(-3)^2-2(c^3+3)=3-2c^3. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}\]
(c) Since \(\alpha\beta\gamma=-1\),
\[\alpha^3\beta^3\gamma^3=-1.\]
The determinant is
\[1-(\alpha^6+\beta^6+\gamma^6)+2\alpha^3\beta^3\gamma^3=2c^3-4.\]
Therefore \(c^3=2\) and
\[c=\sqrt[3]{2}. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1 M1 A1}\]

 Completed

Sources: Cambridge International 9231/11/O/N/2020, Q3; 9231/13/O/N/2020, Q3.





2020 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 1 · 8 marks
Linear transformationUnknown coefficients★★★☆☆
The cubic equation \(x^3+bx^2+cx+d=0\), where \(b,c,d\) are constants, has roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\). It is given that \(\alpha\beta\gamma=-1\).
(a) State the value of \(d\). [1]
(b) Find a cubic equation, with coefficients in terms of \(b\) and \(c\), whose roots are \(\alpha+1,\beta+1,\gamma+1\). [3]
(c) Given also that \(\gamma+1=-\alpha-1\), deduce that
\[(c-2b+3)(b-3)=b-c. \qquad \textbf{[4]}\]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) Since \(\alpha\beta\gamma=-d=-1\), \(d=1\). B1
(b) The transformed roots have
\[e_1'=3-b,\qquad e_2'=c-2b+3,\qquad e_3'=c-b.\]
Thus the required equation is
\[x^3+(b-3)x^2+(c-2b+3)x+(b-c)=0. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}\]
(c) Write the transformed roots as \(r,-r,s\). Their sum gives \(s=3-b\). Also their pairwise sum is \(-r^2=e_2'\) and their product is \(-r^2s=e_3'\). Hence
\[e_3'=e_2'(3-b).\]
Therefore
\[c-b=(c-2b+3)(3-b),\]
which is equivalent to the required result. B1 B1 M1 A1

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231/12/O/N/2020, Q1.




2021



2021 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 3 · 9 marks
Quartic equationPower sums★★★★☆
The equation \(x^4-2x^3-1=0\) has roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\).
(a) Find a quartic equation whose roots are \(\alpha^3,\beta^3,\gamma^3,\delta^3\) and state the value of \(\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3+\delta^3\). [4]
(b) Find
\[\frac1{\alpha^3}+\frac1{\beta^3}+\frac1{\gamma^3}+\frac1{\delta^3}. \qquad \textbf{[3]}\]
(c) Find \(\alpha^4+\beta^4+\gamma^4+\delta^4\). [2]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) Put \(y=x^3\). Since \(x^4=2x^3+1\) and no root is zero,
\[
x=2+\frac1y=\frac{2y+1}{y}.
\]
Cubing and using \(x^3=y\) gives
\[y^4-(2y+1)^3=0,\]
so
\[y^4-8y^3-12y^2-6y-1=0. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}\]
Hence \(\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3+\delta^3=8\). B1
(b) For the transformed equation, \(e_3=6\) and \(e_4=-1\). Therefore
\[\sum\frac1{\alpha^3}=\frac{e_3}{e_4}=-6. \qquad \text{M1 A1 A1}\]
(c) Since \(x^4=2x^3+1\) for every root,
\[\alpha^4+\beta^4+\gamma^4+\delta^4=2(8)+4=20. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]

 Completed

Sources: Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2021, Q3; 9231/12/M/J/2021, Q3.





2021 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 2 · 11 marks
Power sumsPair sums★★★★☆
The cubic equation \(2x^3-4x^2+3=0\) has roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\). Let
\[S_n=\alpha^n+\beta^n+\gamma^n.\]
(a) State the value of \(S_1\) and find the value of \(S_2\). [3]
(b)(i) Express \(S_{n+3}\) in terms of \(S_{n+2}\) and \(S_n\). [1]
(b)(ii) Hence, or otherwise, find \(S_4\). [2]
(c) Use the substitution \(y=S_1-x\), where \(S_1\) is the numerical value found in part (a), to find and simplify an equation whose roots are \(\alpha+\beta,\beta+\gamma,\gamma+\alpha\). [3]
(d) Find
\[\frac1{\alpha+\beta}+\frac1{\beta+\gamma}+\frac1{\gamma+\alpha}. \qquad \textbf{[2]}\]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) \(S_1=2\). Since \(e_2=0\),
\[S_2=S_1^2-2e_2=4. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}\]
(b)(i) From \(2x^3-4x^2+3=0\),
\[S_{n+3}=2S_{n+2}-\frac32S_n. \qquad \text{B1}\]
(b)(ii) Taking \(n=0\) in the recurrence gives
\[
S_3=2S_2-\frac32S_0=2(4)-\frac32(3)=\frac72.
\]
Taking \(n=1\) then gives
\[S_4=2S_3-\frac32S_1=4. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]
(c) Put \(x=2-y\):
\[2(2-y)^3-4(2-y)^2+3=0,\]
which simplifies to
\[2y^3-8y^2+8y-3=0. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}\]
(d) For the new roots,
\[\sum\frac1y=\frac{8}{3}. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231/13/M/J/2021, Q2.





2021 October/November · 9231/11 & 9231/13 · Question 1 · 6 marks
Recovering coefficientsPower sums★★★☆☆
It is given that
\[
\alpha+\beta+\gamma=3,\qquad
\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=5,\qquad
\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3=6.
\]
The cubic equation \(x^3+bx^2+cx+d=0\) has roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\). Find \(b,c,d\). [6]


Show answer and mark scheme

\[b=-(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)=-3. \qquad \text{B1}\]
Using \(5=3^2-2c\) gives \(c=2\). M1 A1
Using
\[p_3=e_1p_2-e_2p_1+3e_3\]
gives
\[6=3(5)-2(3)-3d,\]
so \(d=1\). M1 A1 A1

 Completed

Sources: Cambridge International 9231/11/O/N/2021, Q1; 9231/13/O/N/2021, Q1.





2021 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 4 · 10 marks
Power sumsSummation★★★☆☆
The cubic equation \(x^3+2x^2+3x+3=0\) has roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\).
(a) Find \(\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2\). [2]
(b) Show that \(\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3=1\). [2]
(c) Use standard results from the list of formulae (MF19) to show that
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left((\alpha+r)^3+(\beta+r)^3+(\gamma+r)^3\right)
=n+\frac14n(n+1)(an^2+bn+c),
\]
where \(a,b,c\) are constants to be determined. [6]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a)
\[p_2=(-2)^2-2(3)=-2. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]
(b) Summing the original equation over the roots,
\[p_3+2p_2+3p_1+9=0,\]
so \(p_3=1\). M1 A1
(c) For each \(r\),
\[
(\alpha+r)^3+(\beta+r)^3+(\gamma+r)^3
=p_3+3rp_2+3r^2p_1+3r^3.
\]
Using \(p_1=-2\), \(p_2=-2\) and \(p_3=1\), expand
\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(1-6r-6r^2+3r^3\right). \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}\]
Using the standard sums and simplifying gives
\[n+\frac14n(n+1)(3n^2-5n-16). \qquad \text{M1 M1 A1}\]
Thus
\[a=3,\qquad b=-5,\qquad c=-16.\]

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231/12/O/N/2021, Q4.




2022



2022 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 4 · 8 marks
Reciprocal powersTransformed roots★★★★☆
The cubic equation \(2x^3+5x^2-6=0\) has roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\).
(a) Find a cubic equation whose roots are \(1/\alpha^3,1/\beta^3,1/\gamma^3\). [3]
(b) Find
\[\frac1{\alpha^6}+\frac1{\beta^6}+\frac1{\gamma^6}. \qquad \textbf{[3]}\]
(c) Find also
\[\frac1{\alpha^9}+\frac1{\beta^9}+\frac1{\gamma^9}. \qquad \textbf{[2]}\]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) First put \(t=1/x\). Dividing the original equation by \(x^3\) gives
\[
2+5t-6t^3=0,
\]
so the reciprocal roots satisfy \(6t^3-5t-2=0\). Now put \(y=t^3\). Then
\[
5t=6y-2.
\]
Cubing and using \(t^3=y\) gives
\[
125y=(6y-2)^3.
\]
Expanding and simplifying gives
\[216y^3-216y^2-53y-8=0. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}\]
(b) For the transformed roots,
\[e_1=1,\qquad e_2=-\frac{53}{216}.\]
Therefore
\[p_2=1-2\left(-\frac{53}{216}\right)=\frac{161}{108}. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}\]
(c) If \(z\) is one of the transformed roots, then
\[
216z^3-216z^2-53z-8=0.
\]
Summing this equation over all three transformed roots gives
\[216S_{-9}=216S_{-6}+53S_{-3}+24.\]
Since \(S_{-3}=1\),
\[S_{-9}=\frac{133}{72}. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]

 Completed

Sources: Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2022, Q4; 9231/12/M/J/2022, Q4.





2022 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 2 · 7 marks
Symmetric sumsSingular matrix★★★☆☆
The cubic equation \(x^3+5x^2+10x-2=0\) has roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\).
(a) Find \(\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2\). [3]
(b) Show that
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
1&\alpha&\beta\\
\alpha&1&\gamma\\
\beta&\gamma&1
\end{pmatrix}
\]
is singular. [4]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) \(e_1=-5\), \(e_2=10\), so
\[\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=25-20=5. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}\]
(b) The determinant is
\[1-\alpha^2-\beta^2-\gamma^2+2\alpha\beta\gamma.\]
Since \(\alpha\beta\gamma=2\),
\[1-5+2(2)=0.\]
Therefore the matrix is singular. M1 A1 M1 A1

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231/13/M/J/2022, Q2.




2023



2023 October/November · 9231/11 & 9231/13 · Question 3 · 8 marks
Quartic equationUnknown coefficients★★★☆☆
The quartic equation
\[x^4+bx^3+cx^2+dx-2=0\]
has roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\). It is given that
\[
\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta=3,
\]
\[
\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2+\delta^2=5,
\]
and
\[
\alpha^{-1}+\beta^{-1}+\gamma^{-1}+\delta^{-1}=6.
\]
(a) Find \(b,c,d\). [6]
(b) Given also that \(\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3+\delta^3=-27\), find \(\alpha^4+\beta^4+\gamma^4+\delta^4\). [2]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a)
\[b=-3. \qquad \text{B1}\]
Also
\[5=3^2-2c,\]
so \(c=2\). M1 A1
Here \(e_4=-2\) and \(e_3=-d\). Since the reciprocal sum is \(e_3/e_4\),
\[\frac{-d}{-2}=6,\]
so \(d=12\). M1 A1 A1
(b) Summing the quartic equation over the roots gives
\[p_4-3p_3+2p_2+12p_1-8=0.\]
Hence
\[p_4=3(-27)-2(5)-12(3)+8=-119. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]

 Completed

Sources: Cambridge International 9231/11/O/N/2023, Q3; 9231/13/O/N/2023, Q3.





2023 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 4 · 10 marks
Linear transformationPositive and negative powers★★★★☆
The cubic equation \(27x^3+18x^2+6x-1=0\) has roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\).
(a) Show that a cubic equation with roots \(3\alpha+1,3\beta+1,3\gamma+1\) is
\[y^3-y^2+y-2=0. \qquad \textbf{[3]}\]
The sum \((3\alpha+1)^n+(3\beta+1)^n+(3\gamma+1)^n\) is denoted by \(S_n\).
(b) Find \(S_2\) and \(S_3\). [4]
(c) Find \(S_{-1}\) and \(S_{-2}\). [3]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) Put \(y=3x+1\), so \(x=(y-1)/3\). Then
\[
27\left(\frac{y-1}{3}\right)^3
+18\left(\frac{y-1}{3}\right)^2
+6\left(\frac{y-1}{3}\right)-1=0.
\]
Expanding and simplifying gives
\[y^3-y^2+y-2=0. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}\]
For the transformed roots, \(e_1=1\), \(e_2=1\), \(e_3=2\).
(b)
\[S_2=e_1^2-2e_2=-1, \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]
\[S_3=e_1S_2-e_2S_1+3e_3=4. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]
(c)
\[S_{-1}=\frac{e_2}{e_3}=\frac12. \qquad \text{B1}\]
For the reciprocal roots, the pairwise sum is \(e_1/e_3=1/2\). Hence
\[S_{-2}=\left(\frac12\right)^2-2\left(\frac12\right)=-\frac34. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231/12/O/N/2023, Q4.




2024



2024 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 1 · 6 marks
Pairwise productsUnknown coefficient★★★☆☆
The cubic equation \(2x^3+x^2-px-5=0\), where \(p\) is a positive constant, has roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\).
(a) State, in terms of \(p\), the value of \(\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha\). [1]
(b) Find \(\alpha^2\beta\gamma+\alpha\beta^2\gamma+\alpha\beta\gamma^2\). [2]
(c) Deduce a cubic equation whose roots are \(\alpha\beta,\beta\gamma,\alpha\gamma\). [1]
(d) Given that \(\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=\frac13\), find \(p\). [2]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a)
\[\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha=-\frac p2. \qquad \text{B1}\]
(b)
\[\alpha\beta\gamma(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)=\frac52\left(-\frac12\right)=-\frac54. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]
(c) The new roots have sum \(-p/2\), pairwise sum \(-5/4\), and product \(25/4\). Thus
\[4y^3+2py^2-5y-25=0. \qquad \text{B1}\]
(d)
\[\frac13=\left(-\frac12\right)^2-2\left(-\frac p2\right)=\frac14+p,\]
so
\[p=\frac1{12}. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]

 Completed

Sources: Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2024, Q1; 9231/12/M/J/2024, Q1.





2024 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 2 · 7 marks
Squared rootsPower sums★★★☆☆
The cubic equation \(x^3+2x^2+3x+1=0\) has roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\).
(a) Find a cubic equation whose roots are \(\alpha^2+1,\beta^2+1,\gamma^2+1\). [3]
(b) Find
\[\left(\alpha^2+1\right)^2+\left(\beta^2+1\right)^2+\left(\gamma^2+1\right)^2. \qquad \textbf{[2]}\]
(c) Find
\[\left(\alpha^2+1\right)^3+\left(\beta^2+1\right)^3+\left(\gamma^2+1\right)^3. \qquad \textbf{[2]}\]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) Put \(y=x^2+1\), so \(x^2=y-1\). The original equation can be written as
\[
x(x^2+3)=-(2x^2+1),
\]
hence
\[
x(y+2)=1-2y.
\]
Squaring and using \(x^2=y-1\) gives
\[
(y-1)(y+2)^2=(1-2y)^2,
\]
which simplifies to
\[y^3-y^2+4y-5=0. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}\]
For the transformed roots, \(e_1=1\), \(e_2=4\), \(e_3=5\).
(b)
\[p_2=e_1^2-2e_2=1-8=-7. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]
(c)
\[p_3=e_1p_2-e_2p_1+3e_3=-7-4+15=4. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231/13/M/J/2024, Q2.





2024 October/November · 9231/11 & 9231/13 · Question 3 · 10 marks
Quartic equationHigher power sums★★★★☆
The quartic equation \(x^4+2x^3-1=0\) has roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\).
(a) Find a quartic equation whose roots are \(\alpha^4,\beta^4,\gamma^4,\delta^4\) and state the value of \(\alpha^4+\beta^4+\gamma^4+\delta^4\). [5]
(b) Find \(\alpha^5+\beta^5+\gamma^5+\delta^5\). [3]
(c) Find \(\alpha^8+\beta^8+\gamma^8+\delta^8\). [2]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) Put \(y=x^4\). From the original equation, \(2x^3=1-y\). Raising both sides to the fourth power and using \(x^{12}=y^3\) gives
\[16y^3=(1-y)^4.\]
Hence
\[y^4-20y^3+6y^2-4y+1=0. \qquad \text{B1 M1 M1 A1}\]
Therefore
\[\alpha^4+\beta^4+\gamma^4+\delta^4=20. \qquad \text{B1}\]
(b) Multiplying the original equation by \(x\) and summing over the roots,
\[p_5+2p_4-p_1=0.\]
Since \(p_1=-2\),
\[p_5=-2(20)-2=-42. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}\]
(c) For the roots \(\alpha^4,\beta^4,\gamma^4,\delta^4\), the pairwise sum is \(6\). Thus
\[p_8=20^2-2(6)=388. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]

 Completed

Sources: Cambridge International 9231/11/O/N/2024, Q3; 9231/13/O/N/2024, Q3.





2024 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 3 · 10 marks
Quartic symmetric sumsPower sums★★★☆☆
It is given that
\[
\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta=2,\qquad
\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2+\delta^2=3,\qquad
\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3+\delta^3=4.
\]
(a) Find \(\alpha\beta+\alpha\gamma+\alpha\delta+\beta\gamma+\beta\delta+\gamma\delta\). [2]
(b) Find
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\alpha^2\beta+\alpha^2\gamma+\alpha^2\delta
+\beta^2\alpha+\beta^2\gamma+\beta^2\delta\\
&\quad+\gamma^2\alpha+\gamma^2\beta+\gamma^2\delta
+\delta^2\alpha+\delta^2\beta+\delta^2\gamma.
\end{aligned}
\qquad \textbf{[3]}
\]
(c) It is given that \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\) are the roots of
\[6x^4-12x^3+3x^2+2x+6=0.\]
(i) Find \(\alpha^4+\beta^4+\gamma^4+\delta^4\). [3]
(ii) Find \(\alpha^5+\beta^5+\gamma^5+\delta^5\). [2]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a)
\[e_2=\frac{p_1^2-p_2}{2}=\frac{4-3}{2}=\frac12. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]
(b) Let the required sum be \(T\). Expanding \(e_1e_2\) includes every term in \(T\) once and each triple product three times, so \(e_1e_2=T+3e_3\). Newton’s identity gives
\[4=p_3=e_1p_2-e_2p_1+3e_3=6-1+3e_3,\]
so \(e_3=-1/3\). Also
\[e_1e_2=(\text{required sum})+3e_3.\]
Therefore the required sum is
\[2\left(\frac12\right)-3\left(-\frac13\right)=2. \qquad \text{M1 M1 A1}\]
(c) The monic equation is
\[x^4-2x^3+\frac12x^2+\frac13x+1=0.\]
(i)
\[p_4=2p_3-\frac12p_2-\frac13p_1-4=\frac{11}{6}. \qquad \text{M1 M1 A1}\]
(ii)
\[p_5=2p_4-\frac12p_3-\frac13p_2-p_1=-\frac43. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231/12/O/N/2024, Q3.




2025



2025 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 2 · 7 marks
Cubed-root transformationPower sums★★★☆☆
The cubic equation \(x^3+2x+1=0\) has roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\).
(a) Find a cubic equation whose roots are \(\alpha^3-1,\beta^3-1,\gamma^3-1\). [3]
(b) Find
\[\left(\alpha^3-1\right)^2+\left(\beta^3-1\right)^2+\left(\gamma^3-1\right)^2. \qquad \textbf{[2]}\]
(c) Find
\[\left(\alpha^3-1\right)^3+\left(\beta^3-1\right)^3+\left(\gamma^3-1\right)^3. \qquad \textbf{[2]}\]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) Put \(y=x^3-1\), so \(x^3=y+1\). The original equation gives
\[
2x=-(y+2).
\]
Cubing and using \(x^3=y+1\),
\[
8(y+1)=-(y+2)^3,
\]
which simplifies to
\[y^3+6y^2+20y+16=0. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1}\]
For the transformed roots, \(e_1=-6\), \(e_2=20\), \(e_3=-16\).
(b)
\[p_2=(-6)^2-2(20)=-4. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]
(c)
\[p_3=-6(-4)-20(-6)+3(-16)=96. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]

 Completed

Sources: Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2025, Q2; 9231/12/M/J/2025, Q2.





2025 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 3 · 9 marks
Quartic power sumsStandard sums★★★☆☆
The quartic equation \(x^4+7x^2+3x+22=0\) has roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\).
(a) Find \(\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2+\delta^2\). [2]
(b) Find \(\alpha^4+\beta^4+\gamma^4+\delta^4\). [2]
(c) Use standard results from the list of formulae (MF19) to find
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{10}\left(
(\alpha^2+r)^2+(\beta^2+r)^2+(\gamma^2+r)^2+(\delta^2+r)^2
\right). \qquad \textbf{[5]}
\]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) Since \(e_1=0\) and \(e_2=7\),
\[p_2=0-2(7)=-14. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]
(b) Summing the original equation over the roots,
\[p_4+7p_2+3p_1+88=0,\]
so \(p_4=10\). M1 A1
(c) For each \(r\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(\alpha^2+r)^2+(\beta^2+r)^2+(\gamma^2+r)^2+(\delta^2+r)^2\\
&\qquad=p_4+2rp_2+4r^2
=4r^2-28r+10.
\end{aligned}
\qquad \text{B1 M1 A1FT}
\]
Thus
\[
4\sum_{r=1}^{10}r^2-28\sum_{r=1}^{10}r+100
=4(385)-28(55)+100
=\boxed{100}. \qquad \text{M1 A1}
\]

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231/13/M/J/2025, Q3.





2025 May/June · 9231/14 · Question 4 · 10 marks
Symmetric sumsSingular matrix★★★★☆
The cubic equation \(x^3+bx^2+cx-1=0\), where \(b,c\) are constants, has roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\).
It is given that
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
1&\alpha&\beta\\
\alpha&1&\gamma\\
\beta&\gamma&1
\end{pmatrix}
\]
is singular.
(a) Show that \(\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=3\). [4]
(b) It is given that \(\alpha^3+\beta^3+\gamma^3=3\) and that \(b,c\) are positive. Find \(b,c\). [6]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) The determinant is
\[1-\alpha^2-\beta^2-\gamma^2+2\alpha\beta\gamma.\]
Since \(\alpha\beta\gamma=1\) and the determinant is zero,
\[\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=1+2=3. \qquad \text{M1 A1 M1 A1}\]
(b)
\[3=b^2-2c. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]
Summing the original equation over the roots gives
\[3=-3b+bc+3,\]
so \(b(c-3)=0\). Since \(b>0\), \(c=3\). Substitution gives \(b=3\). M1 A1 DM1 A1

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231/14/M/J/2025, Q4.





2025 October/November · 9231/11 & 9231/13 · Question 4 · 8 marks
Quartic linear transformationPower sums★★★☆☆
The quartic equation \(x^4+x^3+x^2+x+1=0\) has roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\).
(a) Show that a quartic equation with roots \(2\alpha+1,2\beta+1,2\gamma+1,2\delta+1\) is
\[y^4-2y^3+4y^2+2y+11=0. \qquad \textbf{[4]}\]
The sum \((2\alpha+1)^n+(2\beta+1)^n+(2\gamma+1)^n+(2\delta+1)^n\) is denoted by \(S_n\).
(b) Find \(S_2\). [2]
(c) Given that \(S_3=-22\), find \(S_4\). [2]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) Put \(y=2x+1\), so \(x=(y-1)/2\). Substitution and multiplication by \(16\) give
\[
(y-1)^4+2(y-1)^3+4(y-1)^2+8(y-1)+16=0,
\]
which simplifies to
\[y^4-2y^3+4y^2+2y+11=0. \qquad \text{B1 M1 A1 A1}\]
For the transformed roots, \(e_1=2\) and \(e_2=4\).
(b)
\[S_2=2^2-2(4)=-4. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]
(c) Summing the transformed quartic over its four roots,
\[S_4-2S_3+4S_2+2S_1+44=0.\]
Thus
\[S_4=-76. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]

 Completed

Sources: Cambridge International 9231/11/O/N/2025, Q4; 9231/13/O/N/2025, Q4.





2025 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 2 · 8 marks
Recovering coefficientsFourth power sum★★★★☆
The cubic equation \(x^3+bx^2+cx+d=0\), where \(b,c,d\) are constants, has roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\). It is given that
\[
\alpha+\beta+\gamma=2,\qquad
\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=3,\qquad
\alpha^4+\beta^4+\gamma^4=5.
\]
(a) Find \(b,c\). [3]
(b) Find \(d\). [5]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a)
\[b=-2. \qquad \text{B1}\]
Also
\[3=(-2)^2-2c,\]
so \(c=1/2\). M1 A1
(b) Let \(S_n=\alpha^n+\beta^n+\gamma^n\). Summing the original cubic over its three roots gives
\[S_3+bS_2+cS_1+3d=0,\]
so
\[S_3=5-3d. \qquad \text{M1 A1FT}\]
Multiplying the original cubic by \(x\) and summing over its roots gives
\[S_4+bS_3+cS_2+dS_1=0.\]
Substitution gives
\[5-2(5-3d)+\frac12(3)+2d=0,\]
so
\[d=\frac7{16}. \qquad \text{M1 A1FT A1}\]

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231/12/O/N/2025, Q2.





2025 October/November · 9231/14 · Question 2 · 9 marks
Reciprocal relationUnknown coefficients★★★☆☆
The cubic equation \(x^3+bx^2+cx+d=0\), where \(d\ne0\), has roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\) such that
\[\gamma=\frac1\beta.\]
(a) Show that
\[\beta+\frac1\beta=d-b. \qquad \textbf{[3]}\]
(b) Show also that
\[\beta+\frac1\beta=\frac{1-c}{d}. \qquad \textbf{[2]}\]
(c) It is given that \(b=3\), \(c=-3\) and \(d>0\).
(i) Find \(d\). [2]
(ii) Find \(\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2\). [2]


Show answer and mark scheme

Since \(\alpha\beta\gamma=-d\) and \(\gamma=1/\beta\), \(\alpha=-d\). B1
(a) Using the sum of roots,
\[-d+\beta+\frac1\beta=-b,\]
so
\[\beta+\frac1\beta=d-b. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]
(b) Using the sum of pairwise products,
\[-d\beta+1-\frac d\beta=c,\]
which gives
\[\beta+\frac1\beta=\frac{1-c}{d}. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]
(c)(i)
\[d-3=\frac4d,\]
so \(d^2-3d-4=0\). Since \(d>0\), \(d=4\). M1 A1
(c)(ii)
\[\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=b^2-2c=9+6=15. \qquad \text{M1 A1}\]

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231/14/O/N/2025, Q2.

title: 1.2 Rational functions and graphs

title: 1.2 Rational functions and graphs
text:
1. 教材知识点

1.1 Rational functions
有理函数写成
\[
y=\frac{f(x)}{g(x)},
\]
其中 \(f(x)\) 与 \(g(x)\) 是多项式，且 \(g(x)\ne0\)。本章只讨论分子与分母次数不超过 2 的情形。


1.2 Intercepts and asymptotes
作图时依次确定以下信息。

与坐标轴的交点：令 \(x=0\) 求 \(y\) 轴交点；令分子等于零求 \(x\) 轴交点。
竖直渐近线：函数在 \(g(x)=0\) 处无定义时，检查该点两侧的符号与趋向。
水平渐近线：比较 \(x\to\pm\infty\) 时分子与分母的最高次项。
斜渐近线：当分子的次数比分母高 1 时，作多项式除法，将函数写成

\[
y=ax+b+\frac{r}{g(x)}.
\]
当 \(x\to\pm\infty\) 时，余项趋于零，所以斜渐近线为 \(y=ax+b\)。


1.3 A five-step sketching method
教材使用以下五步作图法：

求图像与坐标轴的交点；
求竖直渐近线，并判断曲线在渐近线两侧趋向 \(+\infty\) 还是 \(-\infty\)；
求水平或斜渐近线，并判断曲线从哪一侧接近；
求驻点；
综合所有信息完成草图。



1.4 Range by the discriminant method
把有理函数方程重新整理为关于 \(x\) 的二次方程。对于给定的 \(y\)，图像上存在实点的条件是
\[
\Delta\ge0.
\]
因此，令 \(\Delta<0\) 可以找出函数不能取得的 \(y\) 值；再结合渐近线是否能够取到端点，即可写出值域。


1.5 Symmetry

若 \(f(x)=f(-x)\)，则 \(f\) 是偶函数，图像关于 \(y\) 轴对称。
若 \(f(x)=-f(-x)\)，则 \(f\) 是奇函数，图像关于原点具有二阶旋转对称性。



1.6 The curve \(y=|f(x)|\)
先画 \(y=f(x)\)，再把其中位于 \(x\) 轴下方的部分关于 \(x\) 轴反射。原图上的根保持不变，但通常在根处形成尖点。


1.7 The curve \(y=f(|x|)\)
保留 \(y=f(x)\) 在 \(x\ge0\) 的部分，再把这一部分关于 \(y\) 轴反射。所得图像一定关于 \(y\) 轴对称。


1.8 The reciprocal curve \(y=1/f(x)\)
由 \(y=f(x)\) 作 \(y=1/f(x)\) 时：

两图在 \(y=1\) 与 \(y=-1\) 处相交；
两图在同一 \(x\) 处符号相同；
\(f(x)=0\) 的根通常变成 \(1/f(x)\) 的竖直渐近线；
\(f(x)\) 的竖直渐近线变成 \(1/f(x)\) 在 \(x\) 轴上的间断点；
若 \(f(x)\to L\ne0\)，则 \(1/f(x)\to1/L\)；
\(f\) 增加时 \(1/f\) 减少，\(f\) 减少时 \(1/f\) 增加。



1.9 The curve \(y^2=f(x)\)
方程等价于
\[
y=\pm\sqrt{f(x)}.
\]
因此：

图像关于 \(x\) 轴对称；
当 \(f(x)<0\) 时没有实点；
与 \(y=f(x)\) 在 \(y=0\) 和 \(y=1\) 处相交；
若 \(f(x)\) 的根不是驻点，\(y^2=f(x)\) 通常竖直穿过 \(x\) 轴；
对应驻点的 \(x\) 坐标不变，而 \(y\) 坐标变为 \(\pm\sqrt{f(x)}\)。

2. Textbook examples and examination questions

Textbook Examples


Example 4.1 · Pages 96–97
Let
\[
f(x)=\frac{x^2+1}{x^2+2}.
\]
(i) Sketch the graph of \(y=f(x)\).
(ii) State the range of \(f(x)\).
(iii) The equation \(f(x)=k\) has no real solutions. Find the values of \(k\).


Show solution

There are no real zeros of either \(x^2+1\) or \(x^2+2\). Hence the curve has no \(x\)-intercepts and no vertical asymptotes. It passes through
\[
\left(0,\frac12\right).
\]
As \(x\to\pm\infty\),
\[
\frac{x^2+1}{x^2+2}\to1,
\]
so \(y=1\) is a horizontal asymptote, approached from below. Also
\[
f'(x)=\frac{2x}{(x^2+2)^2},
\]
so the only stationary point is the minimum \(\left(0,\frac12\right)\). The graph is symmetrical about the \(y\)-axis.
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\frac12\le f(x)<1}.
\]
The equation \(f(x)=k\) has no real solutions when
\[
\boxed{k<\frac12\quad\text{or}\quad k\ge1}.
\]



Example 4.1: y = (x² + 1)/(x² + 2)

A minimum at (0, 1/2) and horizontal asymptote y = 1.   Example 4.1: y = (x² + 1)/(x² + 2) -5-4-3-2-1123451xyy = 1(0, ½)

It has vertical asymptotes where \(\cos x=0\), namely

Cambridge examination questions in the textbook


Exercise 4B, Question 4
The curve \(C\) has equation
\[
y=\frac{2x^2+x-1}{x-1}.
\]
Find the equations of the asymptotes of \(C\). Show that there is no point on \(C\) for which \(1<y<9\).


Show solution

Since
\[
\frac{2x^2+x-1}{x-1}=2x+3+\frac2{x-1},
\]
the asymptotes are
\[
\boxed{x=1},\qquad\boxed{y=2x+3}.
\]
Rearranging as a quadratic in \(x\) gives
\[
2x^2+(1-y)x+(y-1)=0.
\]
Real \(x\) requires
\[
(1-y)^2-8(y-1)\ge0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(y-1)(y-9)\ge0.
\]
Thus \(y\le1\) or \(y\ge9\), so no point has \(1<y<9\).

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International AS & A Level Further Mathematics 9231 Paper 11, Question 4, October/November 2014.



Exercise 4B, Question 5
The curve \(C\) has equation
\[
y=\frac{x^2+px+1}{x-2},
\]
where \(p\) is a constant.

Given that \(C\) has two asymptotes, find the equation of each asymptote.
Find the set of values of \(p\) for which \(C\) has two distinct turning points.
Sketch \(C\) in the case \(p=-1\), indicating the coordinates of any intersections with the axes.



Show solution

Polynomial division gives
\[
y=x+p+2+\frac{2p+5}{x-2}.
\]
Hence the asymptotes are
\[
\boxed{x=2},\qquad\boxed{y=x+p+2}.
\]
Also
\[
\frac{dy}{dx}=1-\frac{2p+5}{(x-2)^2}.
\]
There are two distinct turning points precisely when \(2p+5>0\), so
\[
\boxed{p>-\frac52}.
\]
For \(p=-1\),
\[
y=x+1+\frac3{x-2}.
\]
The asymptotes are \(x=2\) and \(y=x+1\). The curve has no \(x\)-intercepts because \(x^2-x+1=0\) has negative discriminant, and its \(y\)-intercept is \(\left(0,-\frac12\right)\).



Exercise 4B Q5: p = −1

No x-intercepts; both branches approach x = 2 and y = x + 1.   Exercise 4B Q5: p = −1 -5-4-3-2-11234567-7-6-5-4-3-2-112345678xyx = 2y = x + 1y = f(x)(0, −½)


No x-intercepts; both branches approach x = 2 and y = x + 1.

Exercise 4B, Question 6
The curve \(C\) has equation
\[
y=\frac{2x^2+kx}{x+1},
\]
where \(k\) is a constant.

Find the set of values of \(k\) for which \(C\) has no stationary points.
For \(k=4\), find the equations of the asymptotes and sketch \(C\), indicating its intersections with the coordinate axes.



Show solution

Differentiation gives a stationary-point equation whose discriminant is proportional to \(2-k\). Hence there are no stationary points when
\[
\boxed{k\ge2}.
\]
For \(k=4\),
\[
y=2x+2-\frac2{x+1}.
\]
Therefore the asymptotes are
\[
\boxed{x=-1},\qquad\boxed{y=2x+2},
\]
and the intersections with the axes are
\[
(-2,0),\qquad(0,0).
\]



Exercise 4B Q6: k = 4

Exercise 4B, Question 7
The curve \(C\) has equation
\[
y=\frac{px^2+4x+1}{x+1},
\]
where \(p\) is a positive constant and \(p\ne3\).

Obtain the equations of the asymptotes of \(C\).
Find the value of \(p\) for which the \(x\)-axis is tangent to \(C\), and sketch \(C\) in this case.
For \(p=1\), show that \(C\) has no turning points, and sketch \(C\), giving the exact coordinates of its intersections with the \(x\)-axis.



Show solution

Division gives
\[
y=px+4-p+\frac{p-3}{x+1},
\]
so the asymptotes are
\[
\boxed{x=-1},\qquad\boxed{y=px+4-p}.
\]
Tangency to the \(x\)-axis requires \(px^2+4x+1=0\) to have a repeated root. Hence
\[
16-4p=0,
\]
so \(\boxed{p=4}\) and the tangent point is \(\left(-\frac12,0\right)\).
For \(p=1\),
\[
y=\frac{x^2+4x+1}{x+1}=x+3-\frac2{x+1}.
\]
Then
\[
\frac{dy}{dx}=1+\frac2{(x+1)^2}>0,
\]
so there are no turning points. The \(x\)-intercepts are
\[
\boxed{\left(-2-\sqrt3,0\right),\quad\left(-2+\sqrt3,0\right)}.
\]



Exercise 4B Q7: p = 4

The x-axis is tangent at (−1/2, 0).   Exercise 4B Q7: p = 4 -4-3-2-1123-7-6-5-4-3-2-112345678xyx = −1y = 4xy = f(x)(−½, 0)


The x-axis is tangent at (−1/2, 0).

Exercise 4B, Question 8
The curve \(C\) has equation
\[
y=\lambda x+\frac{x}{x-2},
\]
where \(\lambda\) is a non-zero constant.

Find the equations of the asymptotes of \(C\).
Show that \(C\) has no turning points if \(\lambda<0\).
Sketch \(C\) for \(\lambda=-1\), stating the coordinates of the intersections with the axes.



Show solution

Since
\[
y=\lambda x+1+\frac2{x-2},
\]
the asymptotes are
\[
\boxed{x=2},\qquad\boxed{y=\lambda x+1}.
\]
Also
\[
\frac{dy}{dx}=\lambda-\frac2{(x-2)^2}.
\]
If \(\lambda<0\), both terms are negative wherever the function is defined, so there are no turning points.
For \(\lambda=-1\),
\[
y=-x+1+\frac2{x-2},
\]
with asymptotes \(x=2\) and \(y=-x+1\). The intersections with the axes are
\[
\boxed{(0,0),\quad(3,0)}.
\]

3. Past-paper question bank

2019



2019 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 10 · 12 marks
Two curvesAsymptotesStationary points
The curves \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) have equations
\[
C_1:\ y=\frac{ax}{x+5},
\qquad
C_2:\ y=\frac{x^2+(a+10)x+5a+26}{x+5},
\]
respectively, where \(a>2\).
(i) Find the equations of the asymptotes of \(C_1\). [2]
(ii) Find the equation of the oblique asymptote of \(C_2\). [2]
(iii) Show that \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) do not intersect. [2]
(iv) Find the coordinates of the stationary points of \(C_2\). [3]
(v) Sketch \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) on a single diagram. You do not need to calculate the coordinates of any points where \(C_2\) crosses the axes. [3]


Show answer and mark scheme

(i) Since
\[
\frac{ax}{x+5}=a-\frac{5a}{x+5},
\]
the asymptotes of \(C_1\) are
\[
\boxed{x=-5},\qquad\boxed{y=a}.
\]
(ii) For \(C_2\),
\[
x^2+(a+10)x+5a+26=(x+5)(x+a+5)+1,
\]
so its oblique asymptote is
\[
\boxed{y=x+a+5}.
\]
(iii) Equating the two functions and multiplying by \(x+5\) gives
\[
x^2+10x+5a+26=0.
\]
Its discriminant is
\[
100-4(5a+26)=-4-20a<0,
\]
so the curves do not intersect.
(iv) Since \(C_2\) is \(y=x+a+5+1/(x+5)\),
\[
\frac{dy}{dx}=1-\frac1{(x+5)^2}.
\]
Thus the stationary-point equation
\[
x^2+10x+24=0,
\]
hence the stationary points are
\[
\boxed{(-4,a+2),\quad(-6,a-2)}.
\]
The sketch must show the common vertical asymptote \(x=-5\), the stated horizontal/oblique asymptotes, the two stationary points of \(C_2\), and no intersection between the curves.

 Completed

Sources: Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2019, Q10; 9231/12/M/J/2019, Q10.





2019 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 6 · 9 marks
Oblique asymptoteStationary points
The curve \(C\) has equation
\[
y=\frac{x^2}{kx-1},
\]
where \(k\) is a positive constant.
(i) Obtain the equations of the asymptotes of \(C\). [3]
(ii) Find the coordinates of the stationary points of \(C\). [3]
(iii) Sketch \(C\). [3]


Show answer and mark scheme

(i) Long division gives
\[
\frac{x^2}{kx-1}=\frac{x}{k}+\frac1{k^2}+\frac{1/k^2}{kx-1}.
\]
Hence the asymptotes are
\[
\boxed{x=\frac1k},
\qquad
\boxed{y=\frac{x}{k}+\frac1{k^2}}.
\]
Also
\[
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x(kx-2)}{(kx-1)^2},
\]
so the stationary points are
\[
\boxed{(0,0)},
\qquad
\boxed{\left(\frac2k,\frac4{k^2}\right)}.
\]
The branch containing the origin touches the \(x\)-axis at \((0,0)\); the other branch has its minimum at \(\left(2/k,4/k^2\right)\). Both branches approach the stated asymptotes.

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231/13/M/J/2019, Q6.

\[
y=\left|\frac{4x^2+x+1}{2x^2-7x+3}\right|
\]
and state the set of values of \(k\) for which
\[
\left|\frac{4x^2+x+1}{2x^2-7x+3}\right|=k
\]
has four distinct real solutions. [2]


Show answer and mark scheme

The asymptotes are
\[
\boxed{x=\frac12},\qquad\boxed{x=3},\qquad\boxed{y=2}.
\]
The quotient rule gives
\[
\frac{dy}{dx}
=\frac{-10(3x+1)(x-1)}{(2x^2-7x+3)^2}.
\]
Hence the stationary points are
\[
\boxed{\left(-\frac13,\frac15\right),\qquad(1,-3)}.
\]
The numerator has no real roots; the only axis intersection is
\[
\boxed{\left(0,\frac13\right)}.
\]
The graph has three branches separated by the two vertical asymptotes. After reflecting the negative parts in the \(x\)-axis, four distinct intersections with \(y=k\) occur when
\[
\boxed{k>3}.
\]

 Completed

Sources: Cambridge International 9231/11/O/N/2024, Q6; 9231/13/O/N/2024, Q6.

Show answer and mark scheme

There are no vertical asymptotes and the horizontal asymptote is

\boxed{y=1}.

Writing
\[
y=1+\frac2{x^2+1}

shows immediately that \(1<y\le3\). Also
\[
\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{4x}{(x^2+1)^2},

so the only stationary point and axis intersection is

\boxed{(0,3)}.

\[
\boxed{-1<x<1}.

Since \(2x^2-7x-4=(2x+1)(x-4)\) and the ratio of leading coefficients is \(1\), the asymptotes are

\boxed{x=-\frac12},\qquad\boxed{x=4},\qquad\boxed{y=1}.

\frac{dy}{dx}
=\frac{-4(x+5)(x-1)}{(2x^2-7x-4)^2}.

\boxed{\left(-5,\frac{25}{27}\right),\qquad\left(1,\frac13\right)}.

The intersections are

\boxed{(0,0),\qquad\left(\frac52,0\right)}.
\]
The boundary equations are \(9(2x^2-5x)=\pm(2x^2-7x-4)\). Solving both quadratics and using a sign chart gives
\[
\boxed{
\frac{13-3\sqrt{21}}{10}<x<\frac{19-3\sqrt{33}}{16}
\quad\text{or}\quad
\frac{19+3\sqrt{33}}{16}<x<\frac{13+3\sqrt{21}}{10}}.

2025 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 6 · 14 marks
ParameterModulus
The curve \(C\) has equation
\[
y=\frac{x^2+a}{x+a},
\]
where \(a\) is a positive constant.
(a) Find the equations of the asymptotes of \(C\). [3]
(b) Find, in terms of \(a\), the \(x\)-coordinates of the stationary points on \(C\). [3]
(c) Sketch \(C\), stating the coordinates of any intersections with the axes. [3]
(d) Sketch
\[
y=\left|\frac{x^2+a}{x+a}\right|.
\]
[1]
(e) Find the set of values of \(a\) for which
\[
\left|\frac{x^2+a}{x+a}\right|=a
\]
has two real solutions. [4]


Show answer and mark scheme

Long division gives
\[
\frac{x^2+a}{x+a}=x-a+\frac{a^2+a}{x+a}.
\]
Hence the asymptotes are
\[
\boxed{x=-a},\qquad\boxed{y=x-a}.
\]
Also
\[
\frac{dy}{dx}=1-\frac{a^2+a}{(x+a)^2}.
\]
Setting this equal to zero gives the stationary-point \(x\)-coordinates
\[
\boxed{x=-a\pm\sqrt{a^2+a}}.
\]
The numerator has no real zero and the \(y\)-intercept is
\[
\boxed{(0,1)}.
\]
For \(|f(x)|=a\), the equation \(f(x)=-a\) becomes
\[
x^2+ax+a+a^2=0,
\]
whose discriminant is \(-3a^2-4a<0\). The equation \(f(x)=a\) becomes
\[
x^2-ax+a-a^2=0,
\]
and has two distinct real roots when
\[
5a^2-4a>0.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{a>\frac45}.
\]

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231/13/M/J/2025, Q6.





2025 May/June · 9231/14 · Question 7 · 16 marks
Range\(f(|x|)\)Inequality
The curve \(C\) has equation
\[
y=\frac{x^2+x-4}{x^2+x+2}.
\]
(a) State the equation of the asymptote of \(C\). [1]
(b) Show that, for all real \(x\),
\[
-\frac{17}{7}\le y<1.
\]
[4]
(c) Find the coordinates of any stationary points of \(C\). [3]
(d) Sketch \(C\), stating the coordinates of the intersections with the axes. [3]
(e) Sketch
\[
y=\frac{|x|^2+|x|-4}{|x|^2+|x|+2}
\]
and find the set of values of \(x\) for which
\[
\frac{|x|^2+|x|-4}{|x|^2+|x|+2}< -\frac12.
\]
[5]


Show answer and mark scheme

The asymptote is
\[
\boxed{y=1}.
\]
Since
\[
y=1-\frac6{x^2+x+2}
\]
and
\[
x^2+x+2=\left(x+\frac12\right)^2+\frac74\ge\frac74,
\]
it follows directly that
\[
\boxed{-\frac{17}{7}\le y<1}.
\]
Furthermore,
\[
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{6(2x+1)}{(x^2+x+2)^2},
\]
so the stationary point is
\[
\boxed{\left(-\frac12,-\frac{17}{7}\right)}.
\]
The intersections are
\[
\boxed{(0,-2),\quad
\left(\frac{-1-\sqrt{17}}2,0\right),\quad
\left(\frac{-1+\sqrt{17}}2,0\right)}.
\]
For \(f(|x|)\), retain the \(x\ge0\) half of \(C\) and reflect it in the \(y\)-axis. Put \(u=|x|\). Then
\[
1-\frac6{u^2+u+2}< -\frac12
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
u^2+u-2<0.
\]
Since \(u\ge0\), this gives \(0\le u<1\), hence
\[
\boxed{-1<x<1}.
\]

 Completed

2025 October/November · 9231/11 & 9231/13 · Question 7 · 14 marks
No stationary pointsModulusInequality
The curve \(C\) has equation
\[
y=\frac{x+2}{x^2+3x+1}.
\]
(a) Find the equations of the asymptotes of \(C\). [2]
(b) Show that \(C\) has no stationary points. [3]
(c) Sketch \(C\), stating the coordinates of the intersections with the axes. [3]
(d) Sketch
\[
y=\left|\frac{x+2}{x^2+3x+1}\right|.
\]
[2]
(e) Find in exact form the set of values of \(x\) for which
\[
\left|\frac{x+2}{x^2+3x+1}\right|>2.
\]
[4]


Show answer and mark scheme

The asymptotes are
\[
\boxed{x=\frac{-3-\sqrt5}{2}},\qquad
\boxed{x=\frac{-3+\sqrt5}{2}},\qquad
\boxed{y=0}.
\]
Differentiation gives
\[
\frac{dy}{dx}
=-\frac{x^2+4x+5}{(x^2+3x+1)^2}.
\]
The numerator quadratic has discriminant \(16-20=-4<0\) and is always positive, so the derivative is never zero. Hence there are no stationary points. The intersections are
\[
\boxed{(-2,0),\qquad(0,2)}.
\]
Solving the boundary equations \(f(x)=\pm2\) and reading the intervals from the modulus sketch gives
\[
\boxed{
-\frac74-\frac{\sqrt{17}}4<x<-\frac52
\quad\text{or}\quad
-\frac74+\frac{\sqrt{17}}4<x<0,
\qquad
x\ne\frac{-3\pm\sqrt5}{2}}.
\]

 Completed

2025 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 7 · 14 marks
Oblique asymptote\(f(|x|)\)Inequality
The curve \(C\) has equation
\[
y=\frac{x^2+x+1}{x+1}.
\]
(a) Find the equations of the asymptotes of \(C\). [3]
(b) Find the coordinates of any stationary points on \(C\). [3]
(c) Sketch \(C\). [3]
(d) Sketch
\[
y=\frac{|x|^2+|x|+1}{|x|+1}.
\]
[2]
(e) Find, in exact form, the set of values of \(x\) for which
\[
\frac{|x|^2+|x|+1}{|x|+1}<3.
\]
[3]


Show answer and mark scheme

Long division gives
\[
\frac{x^2+x+1}{x+1}=x+\frac1{x+1}.
\]
Hence the asymptotes of \(C\) are
\[
\boxed{x=-1},\qquad\boxed{y=x}.
\]
Also
\[
\frac{dy}{dx}=1-\frac1{(x+1)^2}=0
\]
gives \(x=0,-2\), so the stationary points are
\[
\boxed{(0,1),\qquad(-2,-3)}.
\]
For \(f(|x|)\), retain the right-hand branch and reflect it in the \(y\)-axis; the result is smooth at \((0,1)\). Put \(u=|x|\). Then
\[
\frac{u^2+u+1}{u+1}<3
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
u^2-2u-2<0.
\]
Thus \(0\le u<1+\sqrt3\), giving
\[
\boxed{-1-\sqrt3<x<1+\sqrt3}.
\]

 Completed

2025 October/November · 9231/14 · Question 7 · 16 marks
No stationary pointsModulusGiven intervals
The curve \(C\) has equation
\[
y=\frac{10x^2-11x-18}{10x-18}.
\]
(a) Find the equations of the asymptotes of \(C\). [3]
(b) Show that \(C\) has no stationary points. [4]
(c) Sketch \(C\), stating the coordinates of the points of intersection with the axes. [3]
(d) Sketch
\[
y=\left|\frac{10x^2-11x-18}{10x-18}\right|.
\]
[2]
(e) Given that
\[
\left|\frac{10x^2-11x-18}{10x-18}\right|<4
\]
for
\[
\frac{-29-\sqrt{4441}}{20}<x<p
\quad\text{and}\quad
\frac{-29+\sqrt{4441}}{20}<x<q,
\]
find \(p\) and \(q\). [4]


Show answer and mark scheme

Long division gives
\[
\frac{10x^2-11x-18}{10x-18}
=x+\frac7{10}-\frac{27/5}{10x-18}.
\]
Hence the asymptotes are
\[
\boxed{x=\frac95},\qquad\boxed{y=x+\frac7{10}}.
\]
Differentiating this form,
\[
\frac{dy}{dx}=1+\frac{54}{(10x-18)^2}>0,
\]
so there are no stationary points. The intersections are
\[
\boxed{(0,1),\qquad\left(-\frac9{10},0\right),\qquad(2,0)}.
\]
For \(|f(x)|<4\), the four boundary values come from \(f(x)=4\) and \(f(x)=-4\). The two values represented by \(p,q\) come from \(f(x)=4\), giving
\[
10x^2-51x+54=0.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{p=\frac32},\qquad\boxed{q=\frac{18}{5}}.
\]

 Completed

title: 1.2 Rational functions and graphs
text:
4. 完成本节的判断标准
当你能够完成以下任务，本节可以视为基本掌握：

不借助图形软件求出有理函数的全部渐近线、交点和驻点；
使用判别式准确求值域或证明某段值域不存在；
根据关键特征画出各分支，并正确表示渐近行为；
从 \(y=f(x)\) 准确得到 \(|f(x)|\)、\(f(|x|)\)、\(1/f(x)\) 与 \(y^2=f(x)\)；
使用图像求方程解的个数和不等式的精确解集。

title: 1.4 Matrices
text:
重要本节考纲要求



考生需要能够：

对不超过 \(3\times3\) 的矩阵进行加、减、乘运算，并识别零矩阵与单位矩阵；
判断方阵是 singular 还是 non-singular，计算 \(2\times2\)、\(3\times3\) 行列式和非奇异矩阵的逆；
使用 \((AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}\)，并推广到多个矩阵的乘积；
用 \(2\times2\) 矩阵表示旋转、反射、放大、伸缩、剪切等平面变换；
理解复合变换的顺序：\(AB\) 表示先作 \(B\)，再作 \(A\)；
使用 \(|\det M|\) 求面积伸缩因子；
求矩阵变换下的不动点与不变直线。

title: 1.4 Matrices
text:
学习路线


先检查矩阵阶数，再决定加减或乘法是否有定义
能区分 \(AB\) 与 \(BA\)，并准确解释复合变换顺序
能计算 \(2\times2\)、\(3\times3\) 行列式及逆矩阵
能由单位向量的像写出变换矩阵
能从矩阵识别旋转、反射、伸缩、放大和剪切
能用矩阵方程求不动点，并用直线映射条件求不变直线

title: 1.4 Matrices
text:
1. 教材知识点

1.1 Matrix operations
只有阶数相同的矩阵可以相加或相减。若 \(A\) 为 \(m\times n\)，\(B\) 为 \(n\times p\)，则 \(AB\) 有定义且为 \(m\times p\)。
矩阵乘法一般不满足交换律：
\[
AB\ne BA,
\]
但满足结合律与分配律。单位矩阵 \(I\) 满足 \(AI=IA=A\)，零矩阵记作 \(O\)。


1.2 Determinants and inverses
对于
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix},
\]
\[
\det A=ad-bc.
\]
若 \(\det A=0\)，则 \(A\) singular，不存在逆矩阵；若 \(\det A\ne0\)，则
\[
A^{-1}=\frac1{ad-bc}\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}.
\]
对 \(3\times3\) 矩阵可按任意一行或一列展开行列式；逆矩阵可由余子式、代数余子式和伴随矩阵求得：
\[
A^{-1}=\frac1{\det A}\operatorname{adj}A.
\]


1.3 Products and inverse order
若 \(A,B\) 均非奇异，
\[
(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}.
\]
右侧顺序必须反转。对三个矩阵，
\[
(ABC)^{-1}=C^{-1}B^{-1}A^{-1}.
\]


1.4 Matrices as transformations
若
\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix},
\]
则
\[
\begin{pmatrix}x'\\y'\end{pmatrix}
=M\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}.
\]
矩阵第一列是 \(\binom10\) 的像，第二列是 \(\binom01\) 的像。常用矩阵包括
\[
R_\theta=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix},
\]
以及
\[
\begin{pmatrix}k&0\\0&k\end{pmatrix},\quad
\begin{pmatrix}1&h\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad
\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\k&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]


1.5 Successive transformations and area
若先作 \(B\)、再作 \(A\)，复合矩阵为 \(AB\)。矩阵 \(M\) 所表示变换的面积伸缩因子为
\[
|\det M|.
\]
行列式的符号还反映方向是否翻转。


1.6 Invariant points and lines
不动点 \(\mathbf{x}\) 满足
\[
M\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x},
\]
即 \((M-I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf0\)。
若过原点的直线 \(y=mx\) 在变换后仍映到自身，则方向向量 \(\binom1m\) 的像必须仍与 \(\binom1m\) 平行。对于一般直线 \(y=mx+c\)，应把像点代回同一条直线并比较系数。

title: 1.4 Matrices
text:
2. Textbook Examples

Example 1.1 · Page 8
Find
\[
\begin{pmatrix}10&3\\-2&7\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}5\\2\end{pmatrix}.
\]


Show solution

Taking each row against the column gives
\[
\boxed{\begin{pmatrix}56\\4\end{pmatrix}}.
\]

 Completed


Example 1.2 · Page 9
Find
\[
\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\-2&5\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}4&3&0\\-2&-3&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]


Show solution

The product has order \(2\times3\):
\[
\boxed{\begin{pmatrix}-2&-6&3\\-18&-21&5\end{pmatrix}}.
\]

 Completed


Example 1.3 · Page 9
Multiply
\[
\begin{pmatrix}3&2\\-1&4\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}
\]
and state what you notice.


Show solution

\[
\boxed{\begin{pmatrix}3&2\\-1&4\end{pmatrix}}.
\]
Multiplication by the identity matrix has no effect.

 Completed


Example 1.4 · Page 16
Describe the transformations represented by
\[
\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}.
\]


Show solution

The first matrix interchanges the coordinates, so it is reflection in \(y=x\). The second multiplies both coordinates by \(2\), so it is an enlargement of scale factor \(2\) about the origin.

 Completed


Example 1.5 · Pages 16–18
Find the matrices representing:

reflection in the \(x\)-axis;
enlargement of scale factor \(3\) about the origin.



Show solution

Use the images of \(\binom10\) and \(\binom01\) as the columns:
\[
\boxed{\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}},
\qquad
\boxed{\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}}.
\]


      xy O    ST(S) reflection in x-axis, then enlargement ×3


Example 1.5: the reflected image lies below the x-axis and every distance from the origin is tripled.



 Completed


Example 1.6 · Pages 19–20
(i) Find the matrix for anticlockwise rotation through \(\theta\) about the origin.
(ii) Hence give the matrix for an anticlockwise rotation through \(60^\circ\).


Show solution

\[
\boxed{R_\theta=
\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}}.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{R_{60^\circ}=
\begin{pmatrix}\frac12&-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\\[2pt]\frac{\sqrt3}{2}&\frac12\end{pmatrix}}.
\]

 Completed


Example 1.7 · Pages 21–22
The rectangle has vertices \(A(-1,2)\), \(B(1,2)\), \(C(1,-1)\) and \(D(-1,-1)\). Find its image under
\[
\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]


Show solution

Multiplying the coordinate matrix gives
\[
\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\0&1\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}-1&1&1&-1\\2&2&-1&-1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}5&7&-2&-4\\2&2&-1&-1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{A'(5,2),\ B'(7,2),\ C'(-2,-1),\ D'(-4,-1)}.
\]


      xy O   originalimage   x-axis fixed; horizontal displacement is proportional to y


Example 1.7: a shear preserves height and area while slanting the vertical sides.



 Completed


Example 1.8 · Pages 23–24
In a shear \(S\), the \(y\)-axis is fixed and \((1,0)\) maps to \((1,5)\). Find the matrix of \(S\).


Show solution

The images of the basis vectors are \(\binom15\) and \(\binom01\), so
\[
\boxed{S=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\5&1\end{pmatrix}}.
\]

 Completed


Example 1.9 · Pages 29–30
Let \(A,B,C\) represent anticlockwise rotations through \(135^\circ\), \(45^\circ\), \(90^\circ\), respectively.

Write down the matrices.
Verify \(A=BC\).
Calculate \(B^3\) and comment.



Show solution

Using \(R_\theta\) gives the three matrices. Since successive anticlockwise rotations add their angles,
\[
\boxed{BC=R_{45^\circ}R_{90^\circ}=R_{135^\circ}=A},
\]
and similarly
\[
\boxed{B^3=R_{135^\circ}=A}.
\]

 Completed


Example 1.10 · Page 33
Let
\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
(i) Show that \((5,5)\) is invariant. (ii) Find all invariant points.


Show solution

Direct multiplication maps \(\binom55\) to itself. In general,
\[
M\binom{x}{y}=\binom{x}{y}
\]
gives \(2x-y=x\) and \(x=y\). Hence every invariant point lies on
\[
\boxed{y=x}.
\]

 Completed


Example 1.11 · Pages 34–35
Find the invariant lines of
\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}5&1\\2&4\end{pmatrix}.
\]


Show solution

Put \(y=mx+c\) and require the image point to satisfy the same equation. Comparing coefficients gives
\[
m^2+m-2=0,
\qquad
(m-3)c=0.
\]
Therefore \(c=0\) and
\[
\boxed{y=x\quad\text{or}\quad y=-2x}.
\]


      xy O    y = x y = −2x points may move, but each whole line maps onto itself


Example 1.11: an invariant line need not be a line of invariant points.



 Completed


Example 6.1 · Page 137
A shape of area \(8\text{ cm}^2\) is transformed by
\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\3&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Find the image area.


Show solution

\(\det M=6\), so the area scale factor is \(6\). The image area is
\[
\boxed{48\text{ cm}^2}.
\]

 Completed


Example 6.2 · Pages 137–138
The unit square is transformed by
\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}2&3\\4&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Find its image vertices, \(\det M\), and the image area.


Show solution

The four vertices map to \((0,0),(2,4),(5,5),(3,1)\). Also
\[
\det M=2-12=-10.
\]
Hence the image area is \(\boxed{10}\) square units.


      xy O   SM(S) area image = |det M| × area original


Example 6.2: the determinant gives the signed area factor; its absolute value gives the area scale factor.



 Completed


Example 6.3 · Page 138
Given
\[
P=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
Q=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},
\]
find \(\det P\), \(\det Q\), and \(\det(PQ)\).


Show solution

\[
\det P=2,\qquad \det Q=3,
\]
and
\[
PQ=\begin{pmatrix}5&4\\1&2\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\det(PQ)=6.
\]
Thus \(\boxed{\det(PQ)=\det P\det Q}\).

 Completed


Example 6.4 · Page 142
Write down matrices \(A,B\) for rotations through \(90^\circ\) anticlockwise and clockwise, and find \(AB\).


Show solution

\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Then
\[
\boxed{AB=I},
\]
so the two matrices represent inverse transformations.

 Completed


Example 6.5 · Page 144
Let
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}11&3\\6&2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
(i) Find \(A^{-1}\). (ii) If \(A\) maps \(P\) to \(Q(5,2)\), find \(P\).


Show solution

Since \(\det A=4\),
\[
\boxed{A^{-1}=\frac14\begin{pmatrix}2&-3\\-6&11\end{pmatrix}}.
\]
Then
\[
A^{-1}\binom52=\binom1{-2},
\]
so \(\boxed{P=(1,-2)}\).

 Completed


Example 6.6 · Page 148
Find the determinant of
\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}3&0&-4\\7&2&-1\\-2&1&3\end{pmatrix}.
\]


Show solution

Expanding along the top row,
\[
\det M
=3\begin{vmatrix}2&-1\\1&3\end{vmatrix}
-4\begin{vmatrix}7&2\\-2&1\end{vmatrix}
=21-44.
\]
Therefore \(\boxed{\det M=-23}\).

 Completed


Example 6.7 · Pages 150–151
Find the inverse of
\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}2&3&4\\2&-5&2\\-3&6&-3\end{pmatrix}
\]
without a calculator.


Show solution

The determinant is \(-6\). The cofactor matrix is
\[
\begin{pmatrix}3&0&-3\\33&6&-21\\26&4&-16\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Transpose and divide by \(-6\):
\[
\boxed{M^{-1}=\frac16
\begin{pmatrix}-3&-33&-26\\0&-6&-4\\3&21&16\end{pmatrix}}.
\]
Multiplication verifies \(MM^{-1}=I\).

 Completed
